title: How to use the library
body:
The library is Compass's own shelf of project-management know-how: short pages on frameworks, delivery, planning, people, risk, contracts, reporting and closing, plus templates and a glossary. Every page is written in Compass's own words, so it stays short, plain and ready to act on.

## Finding things

Open Library and type in the search box. Results appear as you type, ranked by how well the title and text match, with a one-line extract under each. Accents and capital letters do not matter, so "echeancier" finds "Échéancier". The last word you type also matches as a prefix, so "earn" already finds "earned value". The whole library is stored on your device, so search keeps working offline once you have opened Library once.

## Ask about this page

Each page has an "Ask about this page" button. It opens the copilot with that page as the starting point, so you can ask how to apply it to a project. The page text goes to the model as reference material, never as instructions.

## What else appears here

Lessons you record on personal projects appear under Lessons, so the next project can learn from them. Lessons from work projects never appear here. Imported documents appear under Imports, and imports are for personal use only. Pages link to each other with double square brackets, and a link opens the page in place.

title: PMBOK 6: the five process groups
body:
The sixth edition of the PMBOK Guide (2017) describes 49 processes arranged in two ways: by process group (when in the flow of management a process happens) and by knowledge area (what subject it deals with). The five process groups are Initiating, Planning, Executing, Monitoring and Controlling, and Closing. Many organisations, and much of the PMP exam material written before 2021, still use this structure.

The groups are not phases. They describe kinds of management activity, and they repeat inside every phase of a project.

## Initiating

The question here: should this piece of work exist, and who answers for it? Nothing is spent on design or delivery until a sponsor has said yes and someone is named to lead.

- Main outputs: the project charter (charte de projet), which names the sponsor, authorises the PM and states objectives at a high level; the stakeholder register.
- Telecom example: the sales team has signed a multi-site enterprise network deal; the charter confirms scope, sponsor and target in-service window before any engineering starts.

## Planning

The question here: what exactly are we building, and what route gets us there? This is where a rough promise turns into baselines you can be held to, and it is revisited every time something material changes.

- Main outputs: the project management plan with its scope, schedule and cost baselines; the work breakdown structure; subsidiary plans for quality, resources, communications, risk, procurement and stakeholder engagement; project documents such as the risk register and requirements.
- Telecom example: site surveys feed a schedule that sequences fibre builds, equipment orders and installation windows.

## Executing

The question here: is the planned work actually happening? Most of the budget and the team's hours are spent in this group, so the PM's job is to keep people, vendors and equipment moving in step.

- Main outputs: deliverables, work performance data, change requests, issue log updates, selected sellers.
- Telecom example: field crews install equipment, provisioning configures services, the vendor ships routers.

## Monitoring and Controlling

The question here: are we where the plan says we should be, and if not, what do we do about it? It compares actual results with the baselines and decides which changes are allowed in.

- Main outputs: work performance reports, approved or rejected change requests, verified deliverables (quality control), accepted deliverables (scope validation with the customer), forecasts.
- Telecom example: weekly variance against the installation baseline, a change advisory review of a late design change, the customer's acceptance test on each site.

## Closing

The question here: is it really over, and has everyone agreed that it is? A project that just fades out leaves contracts open, operations unsure and lessons lost.

- Main outputs: the final product or service handed over, a final report, closed contracts, archived records and lessons learned (leçons apprises).
- Telecom example: handover to operations with as-built documents, billing confirmed, vendor purchase orders closed.

## How they overlap in a real project

The textbook diagram draws the groups as overlapping waves, and that is how they behave:

- Executing and Monitoring and Controlling run together for most of the project; you are always delivering and checking at the same time.
- Planning never really stops. Rolling-wave planning details the next few weeks while later work stays coarse, and every approved change sends you back into planning.
- In a phased project, Initiating and Closing happen at every phase boundary: you close the design phase and initiate the build phase, usually at a gate.
- Monitoring and Controlling wraps around all the others, including Initiating and Closing.

A network migration might cycle through all five groups once per wave of sites, while the overall project sits in a single long Executing period.

## In practice

- Check that your project has a signed charter; if not, write a one-page version and send it to the sponsor (commanditaire).
- Confirm you have a baseline to measure against: a dated schedule and a budget, saved and not overwritten.
- Make sure every scope change in the last month went through a change request.
- If a phase just ended, hold a short close: what was delivered, what was learned, what carries over.
- Run the status report for the last two weeks and look for variances you have not acted on.

title: PMBOK 6: the ten knowledge areas
body:
In the sixth edition of the PMBOK Guide, each of the 49 processes belongs to one of ten knowledge areas: a subject a project manager has to handle, whatever stage the project is in. Read across with the five process groups, they form the familiar grid of processes.

## Integration management

The area that ties the others together. It covers the charter, the overall project management plan, directing the work, managing project knowledge, integrated change control and closing. When a vendor delay hits schedule, cost and the customer's go-live at once, integration is where you weigh the trade-offs and decide.

## Scope management

Defining and controlling what is and is not included. It runs from collecting requirements to the work breakdown structure (WBS) and the customer's acceptance of deliverables. On an enterprise install, scope says which sites, which services and which demarcation point; "out of scope" matters as much as "in scope" (portée).

## Schedule management

Turning the work into activities, sequencing them, estimating durations and building a schedule you can control. Telecom schedules are dominated by external lead times: building access, permits, carrier handoffs and equipment delivery. Know your critical path and which dates you do not control.

## Cost management

Estimating, budgeting and controlling cost against a baseline. Earned value lives here. On B2B work, watch the gap between what the customer pays and the cost to deliver, including truck rolls, vendor professional services and rework.

## Quality management

Planning what quality means, assuring that processes will deliver it and controlling the results. In practice: acceptance criteria per service, test plans for turn-up, and checking that the last installs did not fail for the same reason.

## Resource management

Planning, acquiring and leading people and physical resources. You rarely own the people on a telecom project; field crews, engineers and vendor staff are shared. Agree commitments with their managers in advance and confirm them before each window.

## Communications management

Getting the right information to the right people at the right time and in the right form. A communications plan names audiences, content, frequency and channel: weekly status to the customer, daily stand-up with the field team, monthly report to the steering committee (comité directeur).

## Risk management

Identifying, analysing, responding to and monitoring risks, threats and opportunities alike. The risk register and its regular review sit here. Typical telecom risks: late equipment, failed site readiness, a customer change freeze, a dependency on another carrier.

## Procurement management

Buying goods and services from outside: choosing the contract type, selecting sellers, controlling delivery and closing contracts. Vendor statements of work, purchase orders and acceptance of vendor deliverables live here.

## Stakeholder management

Identifying stakeholders, planning how to engage them and managing that engagement. It became a separate area in the fifth edition, a sign that engagement is active work, not a mailing list.

## How 6 and 7 relate

The sixth edition is process-based: it tells you which processes exist, with inputs, tools and techniques, and outputs. The seventh edition (2021) is principle-based: twelve principles and eight performance domains describe outcomes and behaviours, and leave the choice of process to you. Seven does not make six wrong. The knowledge areas map loosely onto the domains (risk to Uncertainty, stakeholders to Stakeholders, schedule and cost to Planning and Measurement), and the processes in six remain a useful toolbox when you need a concrete technique. A practical rule: use seven to decide what matters on this project, and six to find a method for doing it.

## In practice

- Walk the ten areas against your project and mark any with no owner or no artefact.
- Check your WBS reaches work packages (lots de travail) small enough to assign and track.
- Write down the three external lead times that drive your schedule and who you chase for each.
- Confirm your communications plan says who gets what, how often, and in which language.
- Review open vendor deliverables and their acceptance criteria.

title: PMBOK 7: the eight performance domains
body:
The seventh edition of the PMBOK Guide groups the work of managing a project into eight performance domains. They are not phases and not process groups: all eight are active at once, they overlap, and each one has outcomes you can check. Use them as a health check on a live project, one domain at a time.

## Stakeholders

Covers finding the people and groups affected by the project, understanding what they need and keeping them engaged.

- Going well: the customer, operations and vendors know what is coming and when; objections surface in meetings, not in escalations.
- Not going well: a stakeholder appears late with a veto; approvals stall because nobody knew they were needed.

## Team

Covers forming the team, setting norms, building ownership and leadership across it.

- Going well: people raise problems early, own their actions and cover for each other in a crisis.
- Not going well: work waits for the PM to chase it; the vendor team and the internal team blame each other.

## Development approach and life cycle

Covers choosing predictive, adaptive or hybrid delivery, and the phases and cadence that fit the deliverables.

- Going well: the approach matches the work (fixed design for the network build, iterations for the portal), and phases end in clear decisions.
- Not going well: sprints imposed on work that cannot change once ordered, or a rigid waterfall forced on a product nobody can specify yet.

## Planning

Covers organising and coordinating the work: scope, schedule, budget, resources, communications and procurement, refined as you learn more.

- Going well: the plan is credible, baselined, and updated when reality moves; estimates have stated assumptions.
- Not going well: the schedule (échéancier) is a wish list, never updated, and the team works from a different one.

## Project work

Covers running the work day to day: processes, physical resources, procurement, communications and learning as you go.

- Going well: hand-offs between provisioning, field and vendor are smooth; lessons are captured during the project, not only at the end.
- Not going well: constant firefighting, duplicate effort, equipment arriving at the wrong site.

## Delivery

Covers delivering scope and quality that produce the intended value, and getting deliverables accepted.

- Going well: acceptance criteria are agreed up front; the customer signs off without long punch lists; benefits start on time.
- Not going well: deliverables pass internal tests but fail the customer's; scope creeps in without change requests.

## Measurement

Covers choosing measures, tracking performance and acting on what the numbers show.

- Going well: a small set of measures (milestones hit, defects, budget burn, cycle time) drives decisions; the RAG status has a reason behind it.
- Not going well: reports are green until the week before go-live, then red; nobody acts on the metrics collected.

## Uncertainty

Covers risk, ambiguity, complexity and volatility, both threats and opportunities.

- Going well: the risk register (registre des risques) is reviewed every cycle, each risk has an owner and a response, and reserves exist.
- Not going well: risks are logged once and forgotten; every surprise becomes an issue.

## How the domains connect

A weak domain drags the others down. Poor stakeholder engagement shows up as late scope changes (Delivery), which break the plan (Planning) and stretch the team (Team). When one domain looks unhealthy, look for its cause in a neighbouring one.

## In practice

- Score your project on each domain as green, amber or red in five minutes; write one action for every red.
- Check the RAID log has an owner and a response for every open risk.
- Confirm the customer has agreed acceptance criteria for the next deliverable.
- Replace one vanity metric in your status report with a measure you would act on.
- Ask the copilot to review the project against these eight domains.

title: PMBOK 7: the twelve principles
body:
The seventh edition of PMI's PMBOK Guide (2021) moved away from a catalogue of processes and put twelve principles at its centre. They describe how a good project manager behaves, whatever the method, so they work for a predictive network build and an agile portal alike. PMI has since published a newer edition that reorganises this material; check which edition your PMO and your certification refer to before quoting one.

## The twelve principles

**1. Stewardship.** Look after the money, people and reputation you have been trusted with, and act with integrity even when nobody is checking. Your duty reaches past the project to the customer and the company. *Example:* you decline to mark an enterprise circuit as in service for billing before the customer has tested it, even though it would help the month-end numbers.

**2. Team.** Build a team that shares goals, agrees how it works and feels safe raising problems early. *Example:* provisioning, field technicians and the vendor's engineers agree in writing who calls whom when a turn-up fails during a night window.

**3. Stakeholders.** Find stakeholders early and keep engaging them, because their interest and influence change as the work moves. *Example:* the customer's security lead, ignored at kickoff, blocks a firewall change two days before cutover; a stakeholder map would have surfaced them.

**4. Value.** Judge the project by the outcomes it enables, not only by the deliverables it hands over, and recheck that value as things change. *Example:* on a multi-site SD-WAN migration, you sequence sites by contract renewal risk rather than by geography, because retention is the real benefit.

**5. Systems thinking.** A project is a set of moving parts inside larger systems, so a change in one place ripples elsewhere. *Example:* moving a cutover date touches the customer's change freeze, network operations centre staffing, the vendor's truck rolls and the billing start date.

**6. Leadership.** Leadership is a behaviour anyone on the team can show: setting direction, influencing without authority and adapting your style to the person. *Example:* with a vendor PM who keeps missing dates, you start with a frank one-to-one and a recovery plan before escalating.

**7. Tailoring.** Fit the approach, governance and paperwork to the size, risk and culture of the work; use just enough process. *Example:* a three-site fibre install gets a one-page plan and a weekly call, not the full artefact set of a national migration.

**8. Quality.** Build quality into the way work is done instead of inspecting it at the end, and define what "acceptable" means with the customer. *Example:* a site-readiness checklist (power, space, building access, demarcation point) completed before dispatch cuts failed installs.

**9. Complexity.** Complexity comes from people, interacting systems, ambiguity and uncertainty; watch for it and respond with shorter feedback loops. *Example:* a unified-communications rollout across several vendors starts with one pilot site to learn how the pieces really behave.

**10. Risk.** Manage threats and opportunities with responses that are proportionate, owned and timely. *Example:* you order long-lead optical equipment before final design sign-off because the lead time threat outweighs the small cost of a change.

**11. Adaptability and resiliency.** Design the project so it can absorb shocks and recover quickly. *Example:* every cutover has a tested rollback plan and a second installation crew on standby.

**12. Change.** Projects change how people work, so prepare them to adopt the new state, not just receive it. *Example:* a new customer portal ships with admin training for the customer and a short guide for their end users.

## In practice

- Pick the two principles your current project is weakest on and write one action for each in the project's tasks.
- Draw a quick stakeholder map (parties prenantes) and check every name has an owner on your side.
- For your next cutover, confirm the rollback plan has actually been rehearsed.
- Restate the project's value in one sentence and check the next milestone still serves it.
- Ask the copilot to review your plan against these principles and list the gaps.

title: PRINCE2: the seven principles
body:
PRINCE2 is a structured project method from the UK, now owned by PeopleCert, with a current edition published in 2023. It rests on seven principles. They are the non-negotiable part: you can tailor themes, processes and documents, but a project that drops a principle is no longer being run the PRINCE2 way. Each principle below has a plain description and what tends to break when it is ignored.

## 1. Continued business justification

There must be a valid reason to do the project at the start, and it must stay valid all the way through. The business case (dossier d'affaires) is rechecked at every stage boundary, not filed after approval.

What breaks: projects keep running after the deal that justified them has shrunk or been cancelled. A customer reduces a 60-site order to 20 and nobody asks whether the dedicated design team still makes sense.

## 2. Learn from experience

Look for lessons before you start, record them as you go and pass them on at the end.

What breaks: the same failure repeats on every project. Installs keep failing because building access was never confirmed, and each new PM discovers this on their own.

## 3. Define roles, responsibilities and relationships

Everyone knows who decides, who delivers and who assures, and the project board (comité de projet) represents the business, the users and the suppliers. The current edition stresses relationships as well as roles.

What breaks: decisions drift, two managers give the field team conflicting orders, or the vendor has no seat where trade-offs are made. Nobody can say who may approve a change.

## 4. Manage by stages

Split the project into management stages and authorise one stage at a time, planning the next one in detail only when you get near it.

What breaks: a single plan covers two years in false detail; the board commits all the money at once and has no natural point to stop or redirect.

## 5. Manage by exception

Each level of management gets tolerances for time, cost, scope, quality, risk and benefits (the current edition also gives weight to sustainability). Within tolerance, the level below gets on with it; a forecast breach is escalated at once.

What breaks: either micromanagement (the sponsor approves every purchase order) or silence (the PM absorbs a six-week slip without telling anyone until go-live).

## 6. Focus on products

Define what is to be delivered, with quality criteria, before planning the work to deliver it. Product descriptions make acceptance objective.

What breaks: activity is tracked but outputs are vague. The team is "90% done" for weeks, and the customer rejects the handover documents because nobody agreed what they should contain.

## 7. Tailor to suit the project

Fit the method to the size, complexity, risk and context of the project, including the organisation's own standards.

What breaks: either "PRINCE2 in name only", with the vocabulary but none of the controls, or a small install buried in full documentation that nobody reads.

## How the principles work together

Stages give the board decision points; business justification tells them what to decide; exception management keeps them out of the detail in between; product focus makes progress measurable. Remove one and the others weaken.

## In practice

- Re-read the business case for your project and write one line on whether it still holds.
- Agree explicit tolerances with your sponsor: how many days and how much money you may absorb before escalating.
- Write a product description for the next deliverable the customer must accept, with quality criteria.
- Search the library's lessons before planning your next stage.
- Check every board role (executive, senior user, senior supplier) has a named person.

title: PRINCE2: the seven processes
body:
PRINCE2's seven processes take a project from the first idea to formal closure. They split the work between three levels: the project board directs, the project manager manages, and team managers deliver. The processes are not phases; several run in parallel.

## The seven processes

**Starting up a project.** A short pre-project check that the idea is worth initiating. The executive and the PM are appointed, the board is designed, previous lessons are reviewed, and an outline business case and project brief are written, with a plan for the initiation stage. *Telecom example:* a customer asks for a national network refresh; start-up confirms there is a sponsor, a rough scope and enough reason to spend money on planning.

**Directing a project.** Runs for the whole project and belongs to the board. The board authorises initiation, authorises the project, authorises each stage (or an exception plan), gives ad hoc direction, and authorises closure. It does not run the day-to-day work.

**Initiating a project.** The first management stage, where the foundations are laid: the approaches for risk, quality, change and communication, the project plan, the detailed business case, and the controls, all collected in the project initiation documentation (PID). The board's decision to authorise the project rests on it.

**Controlling a stage.** The PM's daily work inside a stage: authorising work packages, reviewing progress, capturing and assessing issues and risks, reporting highlights to the board, taking corrective action within tolerance, and escalating when a tolerance is forecast to break.

**Managing product delivery.** The team manager's side: accepting a work package, executing it, and delivering the products back with their quality checks done. For a telecom project this is often the vendor or field team, so the work package doubles as a clear instruction: products, quality criteria, tolerances, reporting.

**Managing a stage boundary.** Near the end of each stage the PM plans the next stage, updates the project plan and business case, reports on the stage just ending, and records lessons. The board then decides whether to continue. If a stage goes out of tolerance, this process also produces the exception plan.

**Closing a project.** Confirms the products are accepted and handed over, checks performance against the baselines, reviews benefits achieved so far and plans the rest, records lessons, and recommends closure to the board.

## Stage boundaries

Stage boundaries are PRINCE2's built-in decision points, equivalent to the gates in a stage-gate life cycle. At each one the board asks three questions: is the business case still valid, is the next stage plan credible, and are the risks acceptable? Good places for boundaries on a telecom project: after design and before ordering equipment; after a pilot site and before the rollout; before a major cutover. A stage should be short enough to control and long enough to be worth a board decision.

## Management by exception and tolerances

Tolerances are the permitted deviation around a target before the next level up must be told. They are typically set for time, cost, scope, quality, risk and benefits.

- The corporate or programme level sets project tolerances.
- The board sets stage tolerances for the PM.
- The PM sets work package tolerances for team managers.

Inside tolerance, each level gets on with the work and reports routinely. When a breach is forecast, not only when it has happened, the PM raises an exception report to the board with options and a recommendation. The board may approve an exception plan, change scope, or stop the project early. This is what lets a busy steering committee (comité directeur) stay out of daily detail without losing control.

*Example:* the board sets a stage tolerance of ten working days and a small cost percentage. A vendor slips equipment by three weeks. That breaches time tolerance, so the PM escalates at once with options: pay to expedite, re-sequence sites, or move the go-live.

## In practice

- Write down your current stage, its end date and the decision the board must take at its boundary.
- Agree numeric tolerances for the current stage with your sponsor, in an email you can point to.
- Turn the next vendor task into a written work package with products, quality criteria and reporting.
- If any tolerance is forecast to break, draft the exception report now rather than at the next meeting.
- Add a milestone in Compass for each stage boundary, named after the decision the board takes there.

title: PRINCE2: the seven themes
body:
The seven themes describe aspects of project management that need attention throughout the project. Each one answers a question and leans on a set of management products (documents). The 2023 edition calls them practices and adjusts some names, for example "organizing" and "issues"; the content below uses the long-established names, which most teams still recognise.

## Business case: why?

Establishes whether the project is, and stays, worth doing. It holds the reasons, options, expected benefits, costs, timescale, major risks and investment appraisal.

- Management products: the business case, the benefits management approach (how and when benefits will be measured, often after the project ends).
- Telecom angle: benefits are usually revenue retention, new contract value or reduced operating cost; make each one measurable.

## Organisation: who?

Defines the project's management structure and roles. The project board (comité de projet) has three interests: the executive (business), the senior user (those who will use the result) and the senior supplier (those who provide the resources). Below sit the project manager, team managers, project assurance, project support and a change authority.

- Management products: the communication management approach, role descriptions in the project initiation documentation.

## Quality: what?

Defines and checks that products are fit for purpose. Starts from the customer's quality expectations and acceptance criteria and turns them into quality criteria for each product.

- Management products: the project product description, product descriptions, the quality management approach, the quality register (planned and completed quality checks).

## Plans: how, how much, when?

Plans are built from products: identify the products, their dependencies, the activities, estimates and resources. Plans exist at three levels: project plan, stage plan and team plan; an exception plan replaces a plan that has gone out of tolerance.

- Management products: project plan, stage plans, team plans, exception plans, product breakdown and flow.

## Risk: what if?

Identifies, assesses and controls uncertainty, threats and opportunities. Each risk has an owner and, where useful, an actionee who carries out the response.

- Management products: the risk management approach, the risk register.

## Change: what is the impact?

Handles issues (requests for change, off-specifications, problems and concerns) and protects the agreed baselines through configuration management. A change authority may approve changes within a budget delegated by the board.

- Management products: the change control approach, issue register, issue reports, configuration item records, product status account, daily log.
- Telecom angle: a customer adding three sites mid-project is a request for change; a delivered router with the wrong optics is an off-specification.

## Progress: where are we now, and where are we going?

Monitors actual against planned performance, forecasts, and escalates when tolerances are threatened. Reporting flows up: team managers to the PM, the PM to the board.

- Management products: work packages, checkpoint reports, highlight reports, end stage reports, exception reports, end project report, the lessons log and lessons reports.

## How the themes interlock

A change request (Change) is assessed against the business case (Business case), may alter the plan (Plans), introduces new risks (Risk), is approved by the right role (Organisation), is checked when built (Quality) and shows up in the next highlight report (Progress).

## In practice

- Check that your project has a risk register and an issue register, and that they are not the same list.
- Write one product description with quality criteria for a deliverable the customer will sign.
- Name your change authority and the budget it may approve without the board.
- Send a one-page highlight report to your sponsor this week.
- Log three lessons from the last stage while they are fresh.

title: Agile values and principles
body:
The Manifesto for Agile Software Development (2001) is short: four value statements and twelve principles. It was written by software developers, but the ideas carry over to any work where requirements are uncertain and fast feedback is possible, such as a customer portal, a self-serve ordering flow or an automation script for provisioning. This page restates them in Compass's words and groups the principles by theme.

## The four value pairs

Each pair names something the authors preferred, with the item on the right still valued, just less.

- **Individuals and interactions over processes and tools.** Talking to the right person usually solves a problem faster than another form or ticket queue.
- **Working software over comprehensive documentation.** A demo of a working feature tells the customer more than a long specification. In telecom terms, read it as "a working service": a circuit that passes traffic beats a perfect design document.
- **Customer collaboration over contract negotiation.** Work with the customer to find the right result, rather than arguing over the wording of the statement of work.
- **Responding to change over following a plan.** Plans are useful, but when the facts change, the plan should change with them.

Note what the pairs do not say: they do not reject documentation, contracts, processes or plans. A B2B project still needs a signed statement of work and a change process; agile asks you not to hide behind them.

## The principles, grouped by theme

The twelve principles fall naturally into six themes.

### Delivering value early and often

- The customer's first need is something useful in hand soon, followed by a steady flow of more.
- Hand over something that works every few weeks; the shorter the cycle, the sooner you can correct course.
- Measure progress by what actually works, not by documents produced or hours spent.

### Welcoming change

- A late change in what the customer needs is a chance to give them something more useful, not an intrusion to resist.

### People and collaboration

- The people who know the business and the people building the solution stay in daily contact, not only at hand-off points.
- Results depend more on whether the team cares about the outcome than on how closely it is supervised; the manager's work is mostly removing obstacles.
- When information has to move inside a team, talking directly beats documents and long email chains.

### Sustainable pace

- Plan for a rhythm people can keep up for this project and the next; heroics are a warning sign, not a plan.

### Technical excellence and simplicity

- Well-built work is cheaper to change; corners cut now slow down every later change.
- Keep things simple: the work you decide not to do is often the biggest saving.

### Self-organisation and reflection

- Teams that decide how to organise their own work usually produce better designs than teams handed every detail.
- On a fixed rhythm, stop to look at how the team works and change one or two things.

## Where agile fits in B2B telecom

Agile thinking works best where the result can be built, shown and changed in small slices: portals, reporting dashboards, ordering integrations, automation. It fits less well where each step is physical and hard to undo: trenching fibre, installing equipment in a customer's data centre, or a cutover inside a fixed maintenance window (fenêtre de maintenance). Most real projects mix both, which is why hybrid delivery is common. Even on predictive work, several principles still apply directly: short feedback loops with the customer, measuring progress by working services, and regular retrospectives.

## Common misreadings

- "Agile means no plan." It means a plan that is expected to change.
- "Agile means no documentation." It means documentation that someone will use.
- "Agile means faster." It means earlier feedback, which often makes the total faster, but not every sprint.

## In practice

- Pick the next deliverable on your project and ask what the smallest version the customer could try would be.
- Book a 30-minute review with the customer's day-to-day contact to show progress, not slides.
- Hold a short retrospective (rétrospective) with your core team: keep, stop, try.
- Check whether anyone on the team is relying on heroics, and rebalance the work.
- Remove one report or form nobody reads.

title: Hybrid delivery
body:
Hybrid delivery combines a predictive frame (phases, gates, a baselined budget and contract dates) with adaptive delivery inside it (iterations, backlogs, frequent demos). It is the normal state of B2B telecom work: the customer signs a contract with dates, part of the solution is physical and hard to change, and part is software that benefits from short feedback loops. The goal is to use each approach where it fits, not to average them.

## Predictive governance around agile delivery

The outer layer stays predictive because the business needs it:

- A business case and charter approved before money is committed.
- Phase gates where the steering committee (comité directeur) decides go or no-go.
- A milestone plan the customer can see, tied to contract dates and billing.
- Change control on scope that affects price, contract or other teams.
- Regular status reporting in RAG terms.

Inside, the agile teams keep their autonomy:

- The product owner orders the backlog within the agreed scope and budget.
- Teams plan sprint by sprint and show working increments.
- Detailed requirements emerge; only changes that affect contract, budget or milestones go to formal change control.

The PM's job is to translate between the two: sprint outcomes become milestone progress, and gate decisions become backlog priorities.

## Gates, milestones and sprints in one plan

A workable hybrid plan has three layers:

1. **Gates** at the phase boundaries, each with defined evidence (see [[project-lifecycle|the life cycle page]]).
2. **Milestones** for external commitments: equipment delivered, site ready, pilot live, customer acceptance, go-live. These are the dates you report and protect.
3. **Sprints** inside the software workstream, each with a goal. Map the sprint goals to the milestones they serve, so a missed sprint goal shows up as a milestone risk early.

Keep the physical and the digital workstreams on one timeline, so the dependency between them is visible: the portal must be able to order the new service before the first customer site goes live.

## Typical telecom examples

**Network build predictive, portal agile.** A customer is moving 80 branches to a managed SD-WAN service. Site surveys, equipment orders, installs and cutovers follow a predictive plan in waves, because truck rolls, maintenance windows and lead times do not iterate well. In parallel, the customer self-serve portal that shows site status and lets the customer request changes is built in two-week sprints, with the customer's IT team at every sprint review. Gate 3 (go for rollout) needs both the pilot sites working and the portal's minimum feature set accepted.

**Data centre migration with automation sprints.** The migration runs in planned move events, each with a method of procedure and rollback. A small team builds the automation scripts and validation checks in sprints ahead of each move, so every event uses the improved tooling.

**Vendor delivery with an agile integration layer.** The vendor delivers hardware to a fixed contract schedule; the integration with ordering and billing systems is delivered iteratively, with the definition of done including end-to-end order testing.

## Common traps

- **Water-Scrum-fall.** A long requirements phase, sprints in the middle, a long testing phase at the end: the sprints add ceremony without feedback.
- **Two plans that disagree.** The steering committee sees the milestone plan, the teams follow the backlog, and nobody reconciles them.
- **Gates that ask for the wrong evidence.** Asking an agile team for a complete design document at gate 2 forces fiction; ask for a working demo and a release plan instead.
- **Change control on everything.** If every backlog change needs a change request, the agile part stops being agile.

## In practice

- Draw your project on one page: gates on top, milestones in the middle, sprints or work waves underneath.
- Agree with the sponsor which changes need a formal change request and which the product owner can decide.
- Link each upcoming sprint goal to the milestone it serves.
- Add a risk for every dependency between the physical and digital workstreams.
- Invite the customer's IT contact to the next sprint review.

title: Project life cycle and stage gates
body:
A project life cycle is the series of phases a project passes through from idea to close. A stage-gate model puts a formal decision point, the gate, between phases: the project may only move on when the evidence for the next phase is good enough. Gates protect the organisation from spending heavily on work that should have been stopped or reshaped earlier.

## Typical phases

Names vary by organisation; the shape is usually the same:

1. **Concept** (idea, opportunity): is there a problem worth solving or a deal worth pursuing?
2. **Feasibility and business case**: options, rough cost, benefits, risks.
3. **Planning and design**: detailed scope, solution design, schedule, budget, contracts.
4. **Build and test** (or execution): the work itself, including pilots.
5. **Deploy and transition**: cutover, go-live, handover to operations.
6. **Close**: acceptance, lessons, contract and financial closure, benefits handed to an owner.

Predictive projects go through these phases once. Adaptive work repeats the build, test and deploy cycle many times inside one phase; hybrid projects do both.

## Gates: go or no-go

At each gate a decision body, usually the sponsor or the steering committee (comité directeur), chooses one of four outcomes:

- **Go**: proceed as planned.
- **Conditional go**: proceed, but named conditions must be met by a date.
- **Hold or recycle**: more work needed in the current phase before deciding.
- **No-go (kill)**: stop the project and release the resources.

A gate that has never said no is not a gate. The value lies in being willing to stop or redirect.

## What evidence each gate wants

| Gate | Decision | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Gate 1 | Start feasibility | Problem or opportunity statement, sponsor named, rough size |
| Gate 2 | Approve the business case | Options compared, cost and benefit estimates, key risks, charter draft |
| Gate 3 | Commit to build | Approved design, baselined schedule and budget, contracts or POs ready, resources confirmed, risk register reviewed |
| Gate 4 | Go live | Test and acceptance results, cutover and rollback plan rehearsed, operations ready, customer informed, change approval obtained |
| Gate 5 | Close | Customer acceptance, handover to operations signed, open issues transferred, lessons recorded, budget reconciled |

On a telecom project, gate 3 is often the expensive one, because it releases long-lead equipment orders and vendor commitments. Gate 4 typically lines up with the change advisory board's approval for the maintenance window and a final go / no-go call a few hours before the cutover (bascule).

## Making gates useful

- Publish the evidence list before the phase starts, so the team knows what to produce.
- Keep gate packs short: a page of summary, then the evidence.
- Separate the gate decision from the status update; the gate asks "should we continue?", not "how are we doing?".
- Record the decision, its conditions and who decided.
- Re-baseline after a gate if the plan changed.

## How Compass's milestone gates work

In Compass, a gate is a milestone marked as a gate. The marker only says "a go / no-go decision happens here"; it does not record which way the decision went.

- Each project has a list of milestones, each with a name, a due date and a done date. A milestone marked as a gate shows a ◆ before its name on the project page.
- Ticking a milestone done records the date it was met. Untick it if the gate was reopened.
- Milestones appear in the project's timeline, in the portfolio as the next milestone, and in the status report, where each is labelled Done, Late, Due this period or Upcoming.
- The outcome (go, conditional go, hold or no-go) belongs in the project's Decisions log, with its conditions and who decided, so the "why" sits next to the date. Conditions become tasks with due dates; risks raised at the gate go in the RAID log.
- A no-go is a decision too: log it, then update the project's status and RAG reason.

## In practice

- List the gates left on your project, add each as a milestone with its date and mark it as a gate.
- For the next gate, write the evidence list and share it with the team today.
- Check the decision body for that gate: who attends, who decides, and whether they have the authority.
- After the next gate, log the outcome in Decisions within 24 hours.
- Look at the portfolio for any project whose next milestone is a gate within two weeks, and prepare the pack now.

title: SAFe basics
body:
The Scaled Agile Framework (SAFe), from Scaled Agile, Inc., is a large, prescriptive framework for running agile delivery across many teams that build one solution together. It layers lean portfolio management, programme-level planning and team-level Scrum or Kanban into one operating model. Large telecom and enterprise IT organisations often adopt it, so a PM working with IT or digital teams will meet its vocabulary even when their own project is predictive. The current major version is 6.0; details change between versions, so check which one your organisation follows.

## Agile release trains

The core unit is the **agile release train (ART)**: a long-lived team of agile teams, typically somewhere between 50 and 125 people, organised around a value stream such as "business customer ordering" or "network service activation". The train plans, builds, integrates and demonstrates together on a shared cadence. Teams within it use Scrum or Kanban, with iterations of usually two weeks.

When a solution is too big for one train, several trains coordinate in a **solution train**. Above that, **lean portfolio management** decides which large initiatives (epics) get funding, usually by funding value streams rather than individual projects.

## PI planning

Work is organised into **planning intervals (PIs)**, earlier called programme increments: commonly 8 to 12 weeks, often four development iterations followed by one innovation and planning iteration.

**PI planning** is the signature event: everyone on the train, in person or online, over roughly two days.

- Business context and vision are presented, followed by the top features for the coming PI.
- Teams draft their iteration plans, identify dependencies on other teams and raise risks.
- Dependencies and key dates are drawn on a shared board, often called the ART planning board.
- Risks are sorted with **ROAM**: resolved, owned, accepted or mitigated.
- Each team commits to **PI objectives**, and business owners assign them business value.
- The train takes a confidence vote; low confidence triggers replanning before anyone leaves.

During the PI, a **system demo** shows the integrated work each iteration, and the **inspect and adapt** event at the end reviews results and picks improvements.

## Roles

- **Release train engineer (RTE).** Facilitates the train, runs PI planning, manages risks and dependencies across teams. Often the role closest to a traditional programme manager.
- **Product management.** Owns the train's backlog of features and its priorities.
- **System architect.** Guides the technical direction across teams.
- **Business owners.** Senior stakeholders accountable for the business outcome; they assign value to PI objectives.
- **Product owner** and **Scrum master / team coach** at team level, as in Scrum.

## How a PM interacts with SAFe

On a B2B project, the PM is often a customer of one or more trains: you need a feature (for example, a new service type in the ordering portal) by a date tied to a customer contract. Get your feature into the train's backlog before PI planning, attend the relevant breakout or the final plan review, and track the dependency on the planning board. A feature not planned at PI planning will usually wait for the next PI.

## When SAFe is heavier than the problem

SAFe brings real costs: training, new roles, a quarterly two-day event, and a lot of terminology. It can be more than the work needs when:

- The work involves one or two teams; plain Scrum or Kanban with a shared backlog is enough.
- Teams do not actually depend on each other; coordinating them on one cadence adds overhead without benefit.
- The work is mostly physical (installs, builds, cutovers) and cannot be integrated every two weeks.
- Leadership wants the labels but not the decentralised decision-making; the result is waterfall with extra meetings.
- Priorities change weekly; a fixed quarterly plan fights the business rather than serving it.

Lighter alternatives include a simple Scrum of Scrums, a shared roadmap with a monthly dependency review, or Kanban with a portfolio board.

## In practice

- Find out which trains your project depends on and who their RTEs are.
- Check the date of the next PI planning and get your feature request in front of product management beforehand.
- Put each cross-train dependency in your RAID log with the PI it is planned for.
- Treat a train's PI objectives as commitments with uncertainty; add a risk if your go-live depends on one.
- If someone proposes SAFe for a small project, ask which inter-team dependency it would solve.

title: Scrum essentials
body:
Scrum is a lightweight framework for building a product in short, fixed-length cycles called sprints. It is defined in the Scrum Guide (latest revision 2020), which is deliberately brief: it sets out three accountabilities, five events, three artefacts and a commitment for each artefact, and leaves the practices to the team. In B2B telecom it suits software and digital work, such as a customer portal, an ordering API or network automation, far better than physical builds.

## Accountabilities

A Scrum team is small, typically ten people or fewer, with no sub-teams and no hierarchy inside it.

- **Product Owner.** One person who decides what the team builds next and why. They own the product backlog, its order and its goal. A committee cannot do this job; if three managers can reprioritise, nobody owns the backlog.
- **Scrum Master.** Helps the team and the organisation use Scrum well: coaches, removes impediments, keeps events useful. Not a project manager and not a secretary, though a PM can grow into the role.
- **Developers.** Everyone who does the work of building the increment: developers, testers, designers, analysts. They own the sprint plan and the quality of what they deliver.

## Events

Every event is time-boxed. The limits below are maximums for a one-month sprint; shorter sprints usually use shorter events.

- **The Sprint.** A fixed cycle of one month or less, usually two weeks, containing all the other events. A new sprint starts as soon as the last one ends.
- **Sprint Planning** (up to eight hours). The team agrees why the sprint matters (the sprint goal), which backlog items to take, and how it will deliver them.
- **Daily Scrum** (15 minutes). The developers check progress toward the sprint goal and adjust the day's plan. It is not a status report to a manager.
- **Sprint Review** (up to four hours). The team shows what it built to stakeholders and they discuss what to do next. A working session, not a slide deck.
- **Sprint Retrospective** (up to three hours). The team looks at how it worked and picks improvements for the next sprint.

## Artefacts and their commitments

- **Product Backlog** (carnet de produit), committed to the **Product Goal**: an ordered list of everything the product might need, aimed at a longer-term goal.
- **Sprint Backlog**, committed to the **Sprint Goal**: the items chosen for this sprint plus the plan to deliver them, owned by the developers.
- **Increment**, committed to the **Definition of Done**: each piece of finished, usable work. An item that does not meet the definition of done is not part of the increment and is not shown as done.

The Scrum values (commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage) underpin all of this; when trust is low the events turn into theatre.

## Common failure modes

- **Proxy product owner.** The real decision-maker sits elsewhere and the named product owner relays messages. Priorities flip mid-sprint.
- **Daily status meeting.** The daily scrum becomes a report to the PM, runs 45 minutes and nobody adjusts anything.
- **No definition of done.** "Done" means coded but not tested, or tested but not deployed. Velocity looks good while defects pile up.
- **Sprints with no goal.** The sprint is just a two-week bucket of unrelated tickets; the review has nothing coherent to show.
- **Skipped retrospectives.** The first event dropped when the team is busy, which is exactly when it matters most.
- **Scrum for physical work.** Forcing equipment installs and fibre builds into sprints creates fake increments. Use a predictive plan or Kanban there and keep Scrum for the software.
- **Fixed scope, fixed date, fixed team, "but agile".** If nothing can flex, the framework cannot help; be honest that the delivery is predictive.

## Scrum and the PM

On a hybrid telecom project the PM often sits outside the Scrum team: managing the business case, the customer, the vendors and the gates, while the product owner steers the backlog. The sprint review is your best source of real progress; attend it and bring the customer when you can.

## In practice

- Ask who the single product owner on your digital workstream is, and whether they can decide without a committee.
- Read the team's definition of done and check it includes testing and deployment.
- Attend the next sprint review and invite the customer's business contact.
- Put the sprint review dates on your project as milestones so the status report shows them.
- If retrospectives have stopped, offer to facilitate one 45-minute session.

title: The Kanban method
body:
The Kanban method is a way to improve how work flows through an existing process, without first redesigning roles or adding new ceremonies. It grew from lean manufacturing ideas and was shaped for knowledge work by David J. Anderson and others in the late 2000s. You start with what you do now, make it visible, and improve it in small, agreed steps. It suits work that arrives continuously and varies in size, such as service activations, change requests, provisioning queues or a PM's own task list.

## The core practices

### Visualise the work

Put every piece of work on a board whose columns match the real steps the work goes through. Make different types of work look different (for example, customer installs, internal changes, escalations). Hidden work is the first thing a board exposes: requests received by email that never entered any tracker.

### Limit work in progress

Cap how many items may sit in a column (or in the whole system) at once. When a column is full, people finish or unblock something before starting something new. This is the practice that makes Kanban work; a board without WIP limits is just a to-do list with columns. Little's Law explains why: with the same throughput, more work in progress means every item takes longer.

### Manage flow

Watch how items move, not how busy people are. Useful measures are cycle time (start to done), throughput (items finished per week), and age of items in progress. Look for queues: work that piles up waiting for approval, for a vendor or for a site visit.

### Make policies explicit

Write down the rules: what "done" means for each column, who may pull work, how urgent items jump the queue, what the WIP limits are. Explicit policies let people make decisions without asking, and let you change a rule deliberately rather than by habit.

### Implement feedback loops

Hold regular, short reviews. A daily board walk (from right to left, focusing on what is blocked) is the core one; others include a replenishment meeting to choose what enters the board, and periodic reviews of delivery and risk.

### Improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally

Treat each change to the process as an experiment: state what you expect, try it, measure, keep or reverse it.

## How Compass's board maps to it

Compass's board has five columns: New, In progress, On hold, Waiting on and Done.

- **WIP limits** are set per column in Settings, as a whole number from 1 to 99, for New, In progress, On hold and Waiting on; Done has no limit. A fresh install limits In progress to five.
- The limit is a **soft limit**: the column header shows the cards in view against the limit (for example 6 / 5) and turns to the danger colour when it is exceeded, and dragging a card into a full column shows a notice. The move still happens. Kanban works the same way in practice: the limit is a signal to stop and swarm, not a lock.
- **Waiting on** is your blocked-work column. A growing Waiting on count means your flow depends on other people; chase those items before pulling new work.
- **Swimlanes** split the board by project, and the Personal / Work / All filter separates the two kinds of work, so different classes of work stay visible on one board.
- Explicit policies are yours to write: for example, a card enters In progress only when it has a due date and a next action.

## Common mistakes

- Setting WIP limits so high they never trigger.
- Ignoring the limit "just this once" every day.
- Columns that describe people rather than steps.
- No regular board review, so blocked items age silently.

## In practice

- Set an In progress limit on your Compass board that is lower than what you have now, and keep it for two weeks.
- Walk the board from right to left each morning and clear one blocked item first.
- Move everything you are waiting on into Waiting on, with the person's name.
- Write three explicit policies for your board and put them in a note on the project.
- Track how many items you finish per week for a month, then use it to set realistic dates.

title: Earned value
body:
"45% of the budget spent, 50% of the calendar gone" says nothing about health. Earned value management (gestion de la valeur acquise) answers the real question: for the money spent so far, how much of the planned work has actually been finished, and what does that predict for the end?

It needs a baseline that spreads the budget over time by work package, an agreed way to measure progress, and actual costs collected at the same level.

## The measures

- **PV, planned value** (valeur planifiée): the budget for the work that should have been finished by today, according to the baseline.
- **EV, earned value** (valeur acquise): the budget for the work actually finished by today, in budget dollars, not what it really cost.
- **AC, actual cost** (coût réel): what has actually been spent to finish that work.
- **BAC, budget at completion**: the total baseline budget.

Measure EV by a rule agreed in advance: 0/100 (credit only when finished), 50/50 (half at start, half at finish) or units complete (sites installed out of sites planned). The coarser the rule, the smaller the work packages should be.

## The formulas

| Measure | Formula | Reading |
|---|---|---|
| Schedule variance | SV = EV − PV | Negative: behind plan |
| Cost variance | CV = EV − AC | Negative: over budget |
| Schedule performance index | SPI = EV / PV | Below 1: behind plan |
| Cost performance index | CPI = EV / AC | Below 1: each dollar buys less than a dollar of planned work |
| Estimate at completion | EAC = BAC / CPI | Forecast total cost if the current cost efficiency continues |
| Estimate to complete | ETC = EAC − AC | What is still to be spent |
| Variance at completion | VAC = BAC − EAC | Negative: forecast overrun |

EAC has other forms, each with its own assumption:

- **EAC = AC + (BAC − EV)**: the overrun so far was a one-off, and the remaining work will cost what was planned.
- **EAC = AC + (BAC − EV) / (CPI × SPI)**: both cost and schedule pressure will continue, for example when catching up means paying overtime.
- **EAC = AC + a bottom-up ETC**: the team re-estimates the rest, when the original plan no longer describes the work.

The **to-complete performance index**, TCPI = (BAC − EV) / (BAC − AC), is the cost efficiency the remaining work needs to land on budget.

## Worked example

A managed Wi-Fi deployment at 40 customer sites has a budget (BAC) of $400,000, planned evenly at $10,000 per site and four sites a week over ten weeks. EV is measured as units complete: a site earns its $10,000 when it passes acceptance.

At the end of week 5:

- the plan called for 20 sites: **PV** = 20 × $10,000 = **$200,000**;
- 16 sites have passed acceptance: **EV** = 16 × $10,000 = **$160,000**;
- finance reports **AC** = **$180,000**.

Then:

- SV = 160,000 − 200,000 = **−$40,000** (four sites' worth of work behind).
- CV = 160,000 − 180,000 = **−$20,000**.
- SPI = 160,000 / 200,000 = **0.80**.
- CPI = 160,000 / 180,000 = **0.89** (0.888…).
- EAC = 400,000 / 0.888… = 400,000 × 180 / 160 = **$450,000**.
- ETC = 450,000 − 180,000 = **$270,000**.
- VAC = 400,000 − 450,000 = **−$50,000**.
- TCPI = (400,000 − 160,000) / (400,000 − 180,000) = 240,000 / 220,000 = **1.09**.

Reading it: each dollar buys about 89 cents of planned work, and the pace is 20% behind plan. If nothing changes, the project lands $50,000 over. Finishing on $400,000 would need the remaining work to run 9% more efficiently than planned, unlikely without a change of approach. Against the other EAC forms, a one-off overrun gives 180,000 + 240,000 = $420,000, and continued cost and schedule pressure gives 180,000 + 240,000 / (0.888… × 0.80) = $517,500. Present that range, not a single number.

## Limits worth knowing

- SPI drifts back towards 1.0 near the end, because all planned work is eventually earned, even late work. Late in a project, trust the milestone dates more than SPI.
- EV ignores quality. A site that "passed" and then needs a revisit earned value it did not deserve.
- Re-baseline after approved changes, never to hide a variance.

## In Compass

The project record holds planned and spent budget, and the portfolio shows % done. That figure counts finished tasks, all weighted equally, so it is not earned value. When a project needs EV, track PV, EV and AC per period with the cost data and put CPI, SPI and the EAC range in the status report's summary.

## In practice

- Agree the EV measurement rule for each work package type with your finance partner.
- Ask finance how far actual costs lag; a three-week lag skews CPI.
- Calculate CPI and SPI for your largest project this week, even roughly.
- Report EAC as a range from two formulas, with the assumption behind each.
- If TCPI is above 1.1, raise it with the sponsor now rather than at the next gate.

title: Estimation techniques
body:
An estimate is a forecast with uncertainty attached, not a promise. Pick a technique that fits how much is known, then report a range with its assumptions. "Six to nine weeks, if the carrier delivers the circuits by the 15th" is more honest, and easier to manage, than "seven weeks".

## Which technique when

| Technique | Use it when | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|
| Analogous | Early, little detail, a similar past project exists | The past project was not as similar as it looked |
| Parametric | The work repeats and you have a reliable unit rate | A rate taken from a different context |
| Three-point / PERT | Duration or cost is uncertain and the risk is mostly one-sided | Optimistic values that are really "most likely" |
| Bottom-up | The WBS is down to work packages | Missing work, and padding at every level |
| Planning poker | A team estimates its own backlog items | Treating points as hours or comparing them across teams |

## Analogous: "last time it took…"

Take a comparable piece of work and adjust for the differences. If last year's 40-site managed Wi-Fi refresh for a retail chain took five months, a 60-site refresh for a similar customer might start at seven, adjusted for the new customer's slower building access. It is quick and good enough for a business case, but only as good as the comparison: note which project you used and what you adjusted.

## Parametric: unit × quantity

When the work is made of repeated units, multiply a measured rate by the count: installs per crew per day, hours per site survey, cost per kilometre of fibre lateral. With 120 sites, two crews, and a measured rate of 1.5 installs per crew per day, installs take about 40 working days, before weather, access problems and failed site visits. The rate is the weak point: check where it came from and whether it included travel, rework and revisits.

## Three-point and PERT

Ask for three numbers, not one:

- **O**, optimistic: things go well, with no heroics.
- **M**, most likely: what usually happens.
- **P**, pessimistic: realistic trouble, but not a disaster.

Two ways to combine them:

- **Triangular average:** E = (O + M + P) / 3.
- **PERT (beta) estimate:** E = (O + 4M + P) / 6, with a spread of σ ≈ (P − O) / 6.

Example: integrating a customer's ordering portal with a new provisioning API, with O = 10 days, M = 15, P = 26. PERT gives (10 + 60 + 26) / 6 = 96 / 6 = 16 days, with σ = (26 − 10) / 6 ≈ 2.7 days. The triangular average is 51 / 3 = 17 days, because it gives the pessimistic tail more weight. Either way, the answer is above the "most likely" 15: when trouble can cost more than luck can save, the expected value sits to the right of the typical case.

As a rough guide, E ± σ is about a two-in-three chance and E ± 2σ about nineteen in twenty, if the spread behaves roughly like a bell curve. For a chain of tasks, add the expected values. For the chain's spread, add the variances (σ²) and take the square root; adding the σ values directly overstates it, as long as the tasks' risks are independent.

## Bottom-up

Estimate each work package with the people who will do it, then roll up through the WBS: the most accurate method once scope is known, and the slowest. Two traps: work missing from the WBS is missing from the estimate, and safety added at every level compounds. Ask for realistic estimates and hold the contingency in one visible place instead (see [[wbs-and-scheduling]]).

## Planning poker

For agile workstreams, the team estimates backlog items in relative points. Each person picks a card privately, everyone reveals at once, and the highest and lowest explain their reasoning before a second round. The discussion matters more than the number: a 3 and a 13 on one item mean two people pictured different work. Points describe size for one team's planning; turning them into hours or comparing velocity across teams defeats the purpose.

## Ranges over single numbers

- Give ranges, and say which end you would commit to and at what confidence.
- Narrow the range as you learn. An early estimate can easily be off by half in either direction; a range that is still wide just before build is a risk to log.
- Keep the assumptions with the estimate. When one breaks, you know which number to revisit.
- Separate estimate from commitment: the team estimates, the sponsor decides how much buffer to buy.

## In practice

- Re-estimate the riskiest work package on your project with three points and compare the PERT result with the current plan.
- For any repeated unit (sites, circuits, users), check where its rate came from and whether it includes revisits.
- Rewrite your next status report's forecast as a range with one named assumption.
- Log the assumptions behind your two largest estimates in the RAID log.

title: Project charter and business case
body:
The business case and the charter are the two founding documents of a project. They are often confused or merged, but they answer different questions. The business case (dossier d'affaires) asks: should we invest in this at all? The charter (charte de projet) says: this project now exists, here is its mandate, and this person runs it.

## The business case

The business case justifies the investment and is used to keep checking it.

What it holds:

- The problem or opportunity, and why now.
- Options considered, including doing nothing, with a recommendation.
- Expected benefits, stated so they can be measured (revenue protected, new contract value, cost avoided, churn reduced), and when they arrive.
- Costs: one-time and recurring, internal and vendor.
- Timescale and major risks.
- Financial appraisal as your organisation requires it (payback, net present value, margin).

Who owns and signs: the sponsor or executive owns it; finance often reviews it; the investment committee or steering committee approves it. The PM usually helps write it and keeps it current, but does not own the benefits.

On B2B telecom work, the business case is often tied to a customer deal: the sales case says the contract is profitable; the delivery business case must show it can be delivered at the planned cost and margin.

## The project charter

The charter formally authorises the project and gives the PM authority to use resources.

What it holds:

- Purpose and objectives, linked to the business case.
- High-level scope: what is in and, just as important, what is out.
- Key deliverables and success criteria.
- Milestones at summary level and a target end date.
- Summary budget.
- Key stakeholders, the sponsor, and the PM with their level of authority.
- Main assumptions, constraints, risks and dependencies.
- Governance: who decides, how changes are approved, how often the steering committee meets.

Who signs: the sponsor (commanditaire), and often the heads of the groups that supply the people. On customer-facing projects, the customer may sign a parallel kickoff document or the statement of work rather than the internal charter.

## How they differ

| | Business case | Charter |
|---|---|---|
| Question | Is it worth doing? | Who does what, with which authority? |
| Owner | Sponsor | Sponsor, issued to the PM |
| Focus | Value, cost, options, benefits | Scope, objectives, governance, authority |
| Life | Revisited at every gate and after closure for benefits | Mostly fixed once signed; changed through change control |
| Audience | Investment decision-makers | Project team and stakeholders |

The business case comes first, or at least alongside. A charter without a business case authorises work nobody has justified.

## What a weak charter looks like

- Objectives that are activities ("install equipment at 40 sites") rather than outcomes ("40 sites live on the new service by March, with billing active").
- No "out of scope" list, so every customer request becomes an argument.
- Success criteria nobody can measure.
- No named sponsor, or a sponsor who has not read it.
- The PM's authority left unstated: can they approve overtime, move a site wave, sign a vendor change?
- Governance missing: no steering committee, no escalation path, no change process.
- Assumptions hidden, such as building access, customer readiness or a dependency on another team's release.
- Written once for the kickoff deck and never looked at again.

## Keeping them alive in Compass

The project record holds the core of a charter: objectives, in scope, out of scope, success criteria, sponsor, phase, dates and budget. Fill those in at the start, log the charter's sign-off in Decisions, put its main assumptions and risks in the RAID log, and recheck the business case at each gate milestone.

## In practice

- Read your project's charter and rewrite any activity-style objective as an outcome.
- Add three items to the project's out-of-scope field that the customer is likely to ask for.
- Confirm in writing what you may approve without the sponsor.
- Ask the sponsor which benefits the business case promised, and who will measure them after closure.
- Log every charter assumption in the RAID log with an owner.

title: WBS and scheduling
body:
A schedule written straight from a list of activities nearly always misses work. Work in two steps. First, agree on what the project must produce and break it down until every piece can be owned and estimated: that is the work breakdown structure (WBS, structure de découpage du projet). Second, put those pieces in order and find the chain that sets the end date: that is the schedule (échéancier).

## Breaking the work down

Start from deliverables, not departments or verbs. For a managed SD-WAN rollout to 60 customer sites, the first level might be: solution design, equipment, site readiness, site installs, ordering and billing integration, customer acceptance and project management. Each branch splits again until it reaches a work package (lot de travail).

A branch is broken down far enough when:

- one person can own it and name its output;
- you can estimate it without saying "it depends" more than once;
- it finishes within one or two reporting periods;
- someone other than the owner can check that it is done.

You went too far when tasks last an hour or the WBS no longer fits on one page. Number every element (1, 1.2, 1.2.3); on larger projects, add a WBS dictionary entry per work package: description, owner, acceptance check, estimate.

## The 100% rule

The WBS holds all of the work in scope and none of the work outside it. At every level, the children add up to exactly their parent.

Two quick tests:

- **Completeness.** For each element, ask: "if every work package under it is finished, is this element finished?" If the honest answer is "almost", something is missing. The usual gaps are testing, training, documentation, handover to operations, decommissioning the old circuits, and the project management work itself.
- **Boundaries.** Read the charter's out-of-scope list. Nothing on it should appear anywhere in the WBS.

## Putting the work in order

Dependencies (dépendances) say what must happen before what. Most are finish-to-start: the access circuit must be delivered before the router can be turned up. Start-to-start and finish-to-finish links, and lags such as "48 hours of soak testing after install", cover most of the rest.

It also helps to know where each link comes from:

- **Hard logic**, set by physics or the contract: no testing before install.
- **Preferred logic**, a team's habit: challenge it when you need time back.
- **External**: a carrier, a permit, the customer's IT team, another Bell group's release. Log each as a dependency in the RAID log, with an owner on the other side.

## The critical path as a concept

Once work packages have durations and links, add up the durations along each chain from start to finish. The chain with the biggest total leaves no room: a day lost anywhere on it is a day lost on the project. That chain is the critical path (chemin critique). Every other chain has float (marge), slack it can lose before it touches the end date.

What this means in practice:

- Watch critical work more closely than the rest; speeding up anything else does not move the date.
- The path moves. When a side chain uses up its float, it becomes critical. Recheck after every real slip.
- There are two ways to compress. Crashing adds resources, such as a second install crew or overtime, and costs money. Fast-tracking overlaps work planned in sequence, such as starting site surveys before the design is signed, and adds a risk of rework.
- People are constraints too. If one engineer sits on two parallel chains, the true longest path runs through her calendar.

## Buffers

Safety hidden inside every estimate tends to get spent, invisibly. Estimate each work package realistically instead, and hold explicit buffers at a few points you control:

- a **project buffer** before the date you committed to the customer;
- **feeding buffers** where a side chain joins the critical path, for example where the integration work meets the first site go-live;
- **contingency** in the budget for known risks, kept apart from the management reserve that only the sponsor releases.

Report buffer used against work done: half the buffer gone with a third of the work finished is an early warning.

## In Compass

Milestones carry the deliverable dates the customer sees, and tasks carry due dates. The WBS outline template numbers each milestone with the tasks due on or before it and gathers the rest under "Other work". Compass does not draw dependency links, so keep external ones in the RAID log. On a project that allows cloud AI, the copilot's "Plan from scope" preset drafts a WBS with three-point estimates; nothing reaches the board until you tap "Add to the board".

## In practice

- Run the completeness test on your top-level deliverables and add what is missing, starting with testing, training and handover.
- Mark the five work packages you believe are critical; ask the team if they agree.
- Log every external dependency in the RAID log with a named owner on the other side.
- Take the padding out of two estimates and put it into one visible buffer before the committed date.
- Add a milestone for each deliverable the customer will see.
