title: Communication management
body:
Most project communication problems are not about writing well. They come from sending the right message to the wrong people, at the wrong moment, in a format nobody reads. A communication plan (plan de communication) fixes that by deciding in advance who needs what, how often, through which channel and in which language. It takes an hour to draft and saves weeks of "why wasn't I told?".

## Start from the audience

Work from the stakeholder register (see [[stakeholder-management]]), and ask three questions about each group:

1. What decision or action do they need to take, and what do they need to know to take it?
2. What would they be upset to learn late?
3. How do they prefer to receive information, and in which language?

An executive sponsor needs the RAG, the trend and any decision required, on one page. A customer's network team needs the cutover schedule and the method of procedure. Field technicians need site addresses, access contacts and times. Sending all three the same 12-page report serves none of them.

## The plan's columns

| Column | Example |
|---|---|
| Audience | Customer IT director |
| Purpose | Confirm readiness, surface blockers early |
| Content | Progress against milestones, next two weeks, their open actions |
| Format | Short written summary plus a 30-minute call |
| Channel | Email and Teams call |
| Frequency and timing | Weekly, Tuesday morning |
| Language | French, documents bilingual |
| Owner | PM |
| Feedback | Questions logged as actions; read receipts not required |

Add a row for each audience, including the internal ones the plan is most likely to forget: operations, finance and the account team.

## Cadence

Match the rhythm to the pace of decisions, not to habit:

- **Daily** during cutover windows and incident-heavy periods: short, factual, at a fixed time.
- **Weekly** for the core team and the customer's working contacts.
- **Every two to four weeks** for the steering committee (comité directeur), with the pack sent two working days ahead.
- **At milestones and gates** for wider audiences: a short note when something they care about is done.
- **On exception**, at once, whenever a tolerance is forecast to break. Do not wait for the next scheduled report.

Fix the day and the time. A status that arrives every Thursday by noon builds trust; one that arrives "most weeks" invites people to chase you.

## Channels

- **Email**: for anything that must be traceable, such as decisions, approvals and formal notices. Write the subject line as the message: "Decision needed by Friday: second install crew for wave 3".
- **Chat (Teams)**: quick coordination; never the only record of a decision. Copy decisions into the decision log.
- **Meetings**: for discussion, alignment and difficult news. Not for reading a status report aloud.
- **Shared documents and dashboards**: for reference material people pull when they need it.
- **Phone**: for bad news to a sponsor, before it appears in writing.

## Bilingual audiences (EN / FR)

Many Bell customers and teams in Québec work in French, and some audiences expect both languages. A few habits make this manageable:

- Ask each stakeholder their preferred language at kickoff and record it in the plan; do not guess from a name or a city.
- For mixed audiences, decide upfront whether documents are bilingual side by side, French first, or issued in two versions. Be consistent.
- Keep a short project glossary of agreed terms, such as cutover (bascule), change request (demande de changement) and steering committee (comité directeur), so translations stay the same from report to report.
- Budget time for translation and review of formal documents; it belongs in the schedule, not squeezed in the night before.
- In meetings, let people speak in the language they are most precise in, and summarise decisions in both.
- Check legal or contractual obligations about the language of customer documents with the account team rather than assuming.

## In practice

- Build or update the communication plan for your project, one row per audience, and check that operations and finance have a row.
- Fix a day and time for your weekly status and tell the recipients.
- Ask your two most important customer contacts which language and format they prefer.
- Rewrite the subject line of your next three project emails so they carry the message.
- Start a ten-term bilingual glossary for the project.

title: Difficult conversations
body:
Every project has conversations a PM would rather postpone: telling a sponsor the date will slip, holding a vendor to a commitment they are missing, raising a performance problem with someone on the team. Postponing them almost always makes them harder. The aim is not to win, but to leave the room with a shared picture of the facts and an agreed next step.

## Before: prepare on paper

Spend fifteen minutes writing down:

- **Your goal.** What should be true when the conversation ends? "The vendor commits to a recovery plan with dates by Friday" is a goal. "The vendor understands how upset we are" is not.
- **The facts.** Dates, numbers, what was promised and what happened, with sources. Things a camera would have recorded.
- **Your story.** What you have concluded from the facts: "they do not take our account seriously". Label it as a story; it may be wrong.
- **Their likely view.** What pressures are they under? What would they say is the cause?
- **What you can offer and what you cannot.** Know your limits before you start.
- **Your opening sentence**, written out.

Choose the setting: in person or on video for anything serious, privately, with enough time. Never in a steering committee in front of others, and never by chat.

## Opening: say it plainly, early

Name the topic in the first minute, without warming up for ten. A useful shape is: the subject, the facts, why it matters, and an invitation.

> "I want to talk about the wave 2 installs. We planned twelve sites by the 30th and we have five. That puts the customer's go-live at risk. I'd like to understand what's happening on your side and agree a plan."

Avoid opening with your story ("you've been unreliable"). It invites a defence of character instead of a discussion of the problem.

## Listening

Then stop talking. Ask open questions: "What's getting in the way?", "What would you need to make the 15th?". Summarise what you heard before answering: "So the crews were moved to another account and the replacement team needs training. Did I get that right?". People who feel heard are far more willing to commit to a fix. Silence is useful; let it run.

## Separating facts from stories

Both sides arrive with stories. When the conversation heats up, go back to what can be checked: "Let's look at the dates together." Offer your story as a hypothesis, not a verdict: "From where I sit, it looks like our sites lost priority. Is that fair?". Invite theirs the same way. Often the story turns out to be half right, and the fixable half becomes visible.

## Closing: an agreed next step

Do not end on "let's keep an eye on it". End with one specific step, an owner and a date: "You'll send a revised install schedule by Thursday noon with crew names; I'll brief the customer on Friday with it." Summarise it out loud, then confirm it in writing the same day. If you could not agree, say so and name the next step anyway, including escalation if needed (see [[issues-and-escalation]]).

## Three common cases

**With a sponsor (bad news).** Bring it early, with the facts, the impact and options with trade-offs, not just the problem. Make a recommendation. Ask for the decision you need. Sponsors rarely punish early bad news; they remember being surprised.

**With a vendor (missed commitments).** Anchor on the contract and the agreed schedule, but look for the cause before the remedy. Ask for a recovery plan with dates, and agree how progress will be checked. Keep the relationship intact; you will need them next month (see [[vendor-management]]).

**With a team member (performance or behaviour).** Do it privately and soon. Describe the specific behaviour and its effect on the project, not the person's character. Ask for their view; there may be a workload or personal reason you do not know. Agree what changes and when you will check in. If they report to someone else, involve their manager properly rather than going around them.

## In Compass

On a project that allows cloud AI, the copilot's "Prepare a difficult conversation" preset drafts a goal, an opening line, facts versus stories, likely reactions and the next step to agree. Treat it as preparation, not a script. Log the agreed next step as a task with its date, and any decision in Decisions.

## In practice

- Name the conversation you have been postponing and book it within five working days.
- Write your goal, facts and story on one page before you go in.
- Draft your opening sentence and say it aloud once.
- After the conversation, send a written summary of the agreed step the same day.
- Add a task to check the agreed step on its due date.

title: Meetings and governance
body:
Governance is the answer to one question: when something needs deciding, who decides, where, and how fast? Meetings are where most of those answers happen. Too little governance and decisions stall or get made in corridors; too much and the project spends its energy feeding committees. The aim is a small set of forums, each with a clear job, and a written trail of what they decided.

## The usual structure

**Steering committee (comité directeur).** The sponsor and the senior people whose budgets, teams or customers the project touches; on a customer project, often a customer executive too. Its job is direction and decisions above the PM's authority: approving gates, releasing contingency, settling priority conflicts between groups, deciding on changes beyond tolerance. It is not a status meeting. If the steering committee spends its hour hearing what happened last week, the pack should have done that job.

**Project working group or core team.** The PM with the workstream leads (design, network, installs, IT integration, operations, the vendor's PM). Its job is coordination: dependencies between workstreams, next two weeks, blockers, risks. This is where most problems are solved before anyone needs to escalate.

**Workstream meetings and stand-ups.** Owned by the workstream leads, at whatever rhythm the work needs. The PM attends selectively.

**Customer meetings.** A regular slot with the customer's project contact, plus wider reviews at milestones. Keep internal debates out of these; settle them first in the working group.

**Technical or change boards.** Change advisory boards for maintenance windows, architecture review boards for design decisions. These belong to the organisation; your job is to know their deadlines and get your items onto their agendas in time.

## Cadence

| Forum | Typical rhythm | Length |
|---|---|---|
| Steering committee | Every 2 to 4 weeks, plus at gates | 45 to 60 minutes |
| Working group | Weekly | 45 to 60 minutes |
| Customer check-in | Weekly or every two weeks | 30 minutes |
| Cutover calls | Daily or several per day during the window | 15 minutes |

Increase the rhythm in critical periods and say so; reduce it when things are stable. A meeting that has had no decisions or actions for three weeks running should be shortened or stopped.

## Agendas that lead to decisions

Send the agenda (ordre du jour) with the pack at least a day ahead, two for the steering committee. For each item, state what you want from it: "for decision", "for input" or "for information". Put decisions first, while people are fresh, and information last, or in the pack only.

A steering committee agenda that works:

1. Decisions required (with options and a recommendation each).
2. Overall status in one slide: RAG, trend, key milestones.
3. Top risks and issues that need the committee's help.
4. Changes for approval.
5. Next gate and what it will need.

## Minutes, decisions and actions

Minutes (procès-verbal, or compte rendu for less formal meetings) do not need to retell the discussion. They need three things:

- **Decisions**: what was decided, by whom, with any conditions.
- **Actions**: what, who, by when. One owner per action, a real date.
- **Points to follow up**: open questions, with who will bring the answer back.

Send them within 24 hours, while memories agree. Ask for corrections by a deadline; silence after that means accepted.

Decisions and actions must not live only in meeting notes, where they get lost. Keep a decision log (registre des décisions) with date, decision, who decided and the reason, and track actions where the team already looks: the task board, not a separate spreadsheet.

## In Compass

Each project has a Decisions tab: date, text, and a link back when a decision came from a meeting review. When you accept a meeting review into a project, its decisions land there, and you can mark open questions and notes as risks or issues for the RAID log. Actions become tasks on the board. Compass can also produce minutes from a reviewed meeting in Word or Markdown. Gate outcomes belong in Decisions too.

## In practice

- Write one sentence describing the job of each recurring meeting on your project; stop or merge any that do not have one.
- Rebuild your next steering committee agenda with decisions first, each marked "for decision" with a recommendation.
- Check that every action from the last working group has one owner and a date, and is on the board.
- Log the last three decisions that only exist in email into the project's Decisions tab.
- Send minutes within 24 hours for every meeting you chair this week.

title: Stakeholder management
body:
Projects rarely fail because nobody knew what to build. They fail more often because someone with influence was surprised, ignored or quietly opposed. Stakeholder management (gestion des parties prenantes) is the deliberate work of finding those people early, understanding what each one needs from the project, and spending your limited time where it changes the outcome.

## Who counts as a stakeholder

Anyone who can affect the project or will feel its effects. On a B2B telecom deal that list is longer than it first looks:

- **Customer side:** the executive who signed, the IT director who must live with the service, the network team that will run it, procurement, site contacts who hold the keys, security and compliance.
- **Bell side:** the sponsor, the account team who owns the relationship, sales engineering who designed the solution, operations and the assurance teams who take over, finance, legal for contract questions.
- **Third parties:** carriers, equipment vendors, installers, building landlords, sometimes a regulator.

Ways to find the ones you missed: walk the WBS and ask who touches each deliverable; read the contract for named approvers; ask each stakeholder "who else should I be talking to?"; and look at who signed off the last similar project.

## The power / interest grid

Place each stakeholder on two axes: how much they can influence the project (power) and how much they care about it (interest). The four boxes suggest a default approach:

| | Low interest | High interest |
|---|---|---|
| **High power** | Keep satisfied: short, well-timed updates; no surprises | Manage closely: involve in decisions, meet regularly |
| **Low power** | Monitor: watch for changes, light touch | Keep informed: regular, useful information; listen |

The grid is a starting point, not a verdict. People move: a customer's procurement lead with little interest during design becomes very interested when an invoice disputes the contract. A quiet site manager can stop a cutover by refusing access. Revisit the grid at each phase.

## Engagement levels

The grid tells you where someone is; engagement tells you where you need them to be. A common five-step scale:

- **Unaware** of the project or its effect on them.
- **Resistant**: aware and opposed.
- **Neutral**: aware, neither for nor against.
- **Supportive**: aware and in favour.
- **Leading**: actively pushing the project forward.

For each key stakeholder, note the current level and the level you need. The gap is the work. You do not need everyone leading; you need the customer's IT director at least supportive before cutover and the operations manager at least neutral before handover. When someone is resistant, find out what they stand to lose. Often it is workload, control or credibility, and the fix is involvement rather than persuasion.

## The stakeholder register

Keep one table (registre des parties prenantes). Useful columns:

| Column | What goes in it |
|---|---|
| Name and role | Including organisation |
| What they care about | Their interest in their own words, not yours |
| Power and interest | High or low on each, or a 1–5 score |
| Current engagement | Unaware to leading |
| Needed engagement | And by when |
| Approach | How you will close the gap |
| Owner | Who on the team holds the relationship |
| Channel and language | Preferred format, frequency, English or French |
| Last contact | Date, so neglected people stand out |

Keep it private. A register that says "resistant, protects his team's budget" should never end up in a shared folder with the customer.

## In Compass

There is no separate stakeholder table: keep the register as a document in the project, record the sponsor on the project record, and log stakeholder risks (a key approver leaving, a resistant operations team) in the RAID log, where they get a score and an owner. On a work project, Compass encrypts both the document and the RAID rows at rest.

## In practice

- List ten stakeholders on your current project and place them on the grid; look hardest at the high-power, low-interest box.
- For the three with the biggest engagement gap, write one concrete action each for this week.
- Ask your sponsor and the account manager who they think you have missed.
- Add a "last contact" date to every row and call the oldest one.
- Log the stakeholder risk you worry about most in the RAID log with an owner.

title: The RACI matrix
body:
When two people both think they own a deliverable, the work gets done twice or argued about. When each thinks the other owns it, it does not get done at all. A RACI matrix (matrice RACI) settles this before it happens: deliverables or decisions down the side, roles across the top, and one letter in each cell that matters.

## The four letters, as four questions

For each row, ask:

- **R: who is doing the work?** The person or team producing the deliverable. There can be several, but if there are more than two or three, the row is probably too big.
- **A: whose name is on it?** The one person who answers for the result, signs it off and makes the call when the R's disagree. They may also be an R.
- **C: whose input do we need before it is final?** People consulted in both directions, before the work is finished. Every C adds time, so add them on purpose.
- **I: who needs to know once it is done?** People informed after the fact, in one direction. They do not get a veto.

## One A per row

This is the rule that gives the matrix its value. Two A's on a row means nobody is accountable; the decision bounces between them, usually at the worst moment. If two people genuinely share a decision, split the row ("design approval: technical" and "design approval: commercial") or name a tiebreaker.

The A must also have the authority to match. Making a junior engineer accountable for a deliverable that needs a vendor's signature is setting them up to fail.

## A short telecom example

| Deliverable | Sponsor | PM | Solution architect | Install vendor | Customer IT | Operations |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| High-level design | I | C | A/R | C | C | C |
| Site survey reports | | I | A | R | C | |
| Cutover plan per wave | I | A | C | R | C | C |
| Go-live decision | A | R | C | I | C | C |
| Handover to operations | I | R | C | | I | A |

Read it down the columns as well as across the rows. A column full of R's is an overloaded person. A column of nothing but I's may be someone who should not be on the distribution list at all.

## Common mistakes

- **Everyone is a C.** It feels inclusive and grinds every deliverable to a halt. Ask "what would change if we did not ask them?"
- **Rows that are activities, not results.** "Attend weekly meeting" is not a deliverable. Use outcomes: "signed site acceptance".
- **No A on a row.** That is usually the row that will slip.
- **The PM as A on everything.** The PM is accountable for the plan and the process, not for every technical decision. Put the A where the expertise and authority sit.
- **Built once and filed.** People join and leave, vendors change. Review the matrix at each phase and whenever a role changes hands.
- **Agreed by nobody.** A RACI written by the PM alone is a guess. Walk it through with the people named and get their nod, especially for every A.

## RACI vs RASCI

Some organisations add **S, support**: people who help the R's with resources or specialist work, without owning the result. On a telecom rollout that might be the logistics team shipping equipment or a security group running a scan. It is useful when a lot of supporting work would otherwise be invisible, and adds clutter when it is not. Variants such as RACI-VS (verify, sign) or DACI (driver, approver) exist for the same reason: pick one and use it consistently across the project.

## In Compass

Compass generates a RACI template from the project: its milestones become the rows (or five blank deliverables when there are none) and the columns are sponsor, project manager, team, vendor and operations, ready for you to fill in. Keep the agreed version with the project, and record in Decisions any RACI change that moves an A.

## In practice

- List the ten deliverables or decisions most likely to cause friction on your project and build the matrix for them.
- Check every row has exactly one A, and that each A has the authority to sign.
- Read each column and rebalance any person with more than four R's.
- Walk the matrix through with the vendor and the customer's IT lead and get their agreement.
- Remove at least two C's that add delay without changing outcomes.

title: Change control
body:
Change is normal on any project that lasts more than a few weeks: the customer adds sites, a vendor discontinues a model, a security review asks for a new firewall rule set. The danger is not change itself but change that slips in without anyone weighing its cost. Change control (maîtrise des changements) is the small, fixed routine that makes every significant change visible, assessed and decided by someone with the authority to decide, before the work starts.

## Baselines: what you change against

You can only control change against something agreed. The baselines are the approved versions of:

- **Scope**: the deliverables and the WBS, including what is out of scope.
- **Schedule**: the milestone dates and the plan behind them.
- **Cost**: the budget, spread over time.

Once a baseline is approved, usually at a gate, it changes only through an approved change request. Progress is measured against it, so moving it quietly every time something slips hides exactly the information the sponsor needs. Re-baseline when an approved change requires it, and record which change caused it.

## Tolerances: what the PM may absorb

Not every variation should go to a board. Tolerances (tolérances) set how far the project may drift before it needs a decision from higher up. For example: schedule ± 5 working days on any customer milestone, cost ± 5% of the budget, no change to contractual scope without the sponsor. Within tolerance, the PM decides and records it. When a change would push the project beyond tolerance, it goes to the sponsor or the change board, and if the project is forecast to break tolerance anyway, an exception report goes up (see [[exception-reports]]).

Agree the numbers in writing at the start. "Use your judgement" is not a tolerance.

## The change request

Anyone can raise a change request (demande de changement). It should say:

- **What** is being asked for and **why**, and who asked.
- **Impact on scope**: what is added, removed or altered, including knock-on effects on other deliverables.
- **Impact on time**: which milestones move and by how much.
- **Impact on cost**: one-time and recurring, internal and vendor, and who pays. On customer projects, whether this is billable under the contract.
- **Other effects**: on risk, quality, operations after handover, other projects.
- **Options**: including not doing it, or doing it later as a separate phase.
- **Recommendation**.

The PM's job is to get an honest impact assessment from the people who will do the work, quickly. A change request that waits three weeks for an estimate is a change control process that people will learn to bypass.

## The change board

Decisions go to whoever holds the authority for the size of the change: the PM within tolerance, the sponsor above it, the steering committee or a formal change control board (comité des changements) for large or contractual changes. On customer projects, contractual changes usually also need a signed amendment or change order with the customer, which the account team owns.

The board can approve, reject, or defer pending more information. Each outcome is recorded with its date and who decided. Approved changes then update the baselines, the plan, the RAID log and the communications; rejected ones are communicated back to the requester with the reason.

Keep the routine proportionate. On a hybrid project, backlog changes inside the agreed scope and budget belong to the product owner, not the change board (see [[hybrid-delivery]]).

## Common failures

- **Change by email.** A customer asks a site engineer for "one small extra" and it is done. Fifty small extras later, the budget is gone.
- **Assessing only cost.** Schedule and risk impacts are often larger.
- **No record of rejections**, so the same request comes back every month.
- **Approving without re-planning**: the change is accepted but the dates and the budget stay the same.

## In Compass

The project's Changes tab holds each request: title, decision (pending, approved or rejected), approver, and an expandable block for the description and the three impacts on scope, time and cost. Setting a decision to approved or rejected records the decision date; setting it back to pending clears it. The portfolio counts pending changes per project, the status report lists pending changes under "Decisions needed", and the change request template builds a document from any change.

## In practice

- Write down your project's tolerances for schedule, cost and scope, and get the sponsor's agreement by email.
- Log every change agreed informally in the last month as a change request, even after the fact.
- For each pending request, check that all three impacts are filled in.
- Agree with the account team how contractual changes reach the customer for signature.
- Tell the team, and the customer's contacts, that any extra request goes through you.

title: Issues and escalation
body:
An issue (problème) is something already going wrong that the project has to deal with: a delivery missed, a test failed, a site refused, a key person gone. Most issues are solved inside the team. The skill is in knowing quickly which ones are not, and moving those to someone with the authority to fix them, before the delay becomes the bigger problem. That move is escalation (escalade), and done well it is a normal tool of management, not an admission of failure.

## Severity: how bad, how fast

Rate each issue on a simple scale agreed with the sponsor at the start, so nobody argues about labels in the middle of a crisis:

| Severity | Meaning | Typical response time |
|---|---|---|
| Critical | Stops the project or a customer service, or breaks a contract date or a tolerance | Same day, sponsor informed |
| High | Threatens a milestone or the budget if not resolved within days | Within two working days |
| Medium | Causes delay or extra effort but can be absorbed | Within the week, through the working group |
| Low | Nuisance; fix when convenient | Next review |

Two questions sharpen the rating: what does this cost per day it stays open, and when does it start affecting something the customer sees? An issue that is "medium" today can become critical in a week because the maintenance window is approaching.

## Escalation paths and thresholds

Agree the path before you need it, in the charter or the governance plan:

1. **Inside the team**: workstream lead and PM, solved in the working group.
2. **To the sponsor**: when the fix needs authority, money or people the PM does not have, or when a tolerance is forecast to break.
3. **To the steering committee**: when it needs a decision across groups, a change to scope, date or budget beyond the sponsor's own tolerance, or a call on the customer relationship.
4. **Across organisations**: vendor issues follow the contract's path, usually vendor PM, then account manager, then a named executive. Customer issues go through the account team, never around it.

Thresholds turn "should I escalate?" into a check rather than a judgement call made under stress. Typical examples: a milestone forecast to slip by more than five working days; a cost impact above an agreed amount; any critical-severity issue; an issue with no owner after 48 hours; a vendor that has missed two recovery dates. When an issue crosses a threshold, escalate, even if you think the team can still save it. Tell the sponsor what you are doing about it at the same time.

## Escalating well

- **Warn before you escalate.** Tell the person whose area you are escalating about, so nobody is ambushed.
- **Escalate the problem, not the person.**
- **Bring options**, not just the problem.
- **Ask for something specific**: a decision, a resource, a phone call to the vendor's executive.
- **Set a deadline** that matches the impact.
- **Close the loop.** When it is resolved, say so to everyone who heard about it.

## Writing an escalation note

Keep it to one screen. A shape that works:

- **Subject**: the ask and the deadline. "Decision needed by Thursday: approve a second install crew for wave 3."
- **What happened**: two or three sentences of facts, with dates.
- **Impact**: on milestones, cost, the customer, in numbers where possible. Say what happens if nothing is done and when.
- **What we have tried**: so the reader knows this is not the first step.
- **Options**: two or three, each with cost, time and risk.
- **Recommendation and ask**: which option, and exactly what you need from the reader, by when.

Example, in brief: the vendor has missed the equipment delivery for 18 sites by two weeks; go-live for the customer's head office slips from the 14th to the 28th unless we act; we have asked for a recovery date twice; options are to wait, to source 6 units from another distributor at $12,000 extra to protect head office, or to resequence waves; recommendation: the second, with approval needed by Wednesday to hold the installer's slot.

## In Compass

Log issues in the RAID tab with impact, owner, response and due date, and use "Make a task" for the actions. Record the escalation's outcome in Decisions. On a project that allows cloud AI, the copilot's "Escalation note" preset drafts the ask, the impact, the deadline and the options for you to edit.

## In practice

- Agree severity levels and escalation thresholds with your sponsor and put them in writing.
- Check every open issue has an owner, a response and a date; escalate any without an owner after 48 hours.
- Write down the vendor's escalation path from the contract, with names.
- Rewrite your last escalation email using the structure above and compare.
- Close the loop on any issue you escalated that has since been resolved.

title: Risk management
body:
Every plan rests on things that might not go as expected: a carrier's circuit arrives late, a customer site is not ready, a vendor's firmware has a bug, or, on the bright side, a second crew becomes free early. Risk management (gestion des risques) is the habit of asking, on a fixed rhythm: what could happen, how likely is it, how much would it hurt or help, and what are we doing about it? Its value is in acting before the event, while options are still cheap.

## Identify

Cast wide, then filter. Useful sources:

- The WBS: walk each branch and ask what could stop or slow it.
- Assumptions in the charter and estimates: each one is a risk if it turns out false.
- Dependencies on carriers, vendors, other teams, the customer, permits and landlords.
- Lessons from similar projects, your own and others' (see [[lessons-learned]]).
- The team, in a short session where nobody is judged for raising an awkward risk.

Write each risk so it can be acted on. A format that helps is cause, event, effect: "Because the building's riser is shared with another tenant (cause), access for the fibre lateral may be refused (event), delaying site 14's go-live by up to six weeks (effect)." Vague risks such as "vendor issues" or "resources" cannot be owned or measured.

## Analyse: probability × impact

Score each risk on two scales of 1 to 5:

- **Probability**: 1 is very unlikely, 5 is almost certain.
- **Impact**: 1 is minor, 5 is severe. Define what each level means for your project in schedule, cost, quality and customer terms, so two people score the same risk the same way. For example: 3 is "a milestone slips up to two weeks or costs up to 5% of the budget"; 5 is "the contract date is missed or the customer escalates to executives".

Multiply them for a score from 1 to 25 and place the risk on a 5 × 5 grid. A common reading is: 15 and above, act now and report to the sponsor; 8 to 14, plan a response and watch it; below 8, note it and review it. Scores are a way to rank and discuss, not precise measurements. Large projects sometimes add quantitative analysis, such as Monte Carlo simulation of the schedule, once the main risks are known.

## Respond

For threats, four main strategies:

- **Avoid**: change the plan so the risk cannot happen, such as choosing a different site entry or dropping an unproven feature.
- **Transfer**: move the consequence to another party, through a contract clause, a penalty, or insurance. The risk still exists; someone else pays for it.
- **Mitigate**: reduce its probability or impact, such as ordering long-lead equipment early or piloting at two sites first.
- **Accept**: do nothing now, either passively or with a contingency reserve and a fallback plan ready.

PMBOK 6 also names **escalate**, for threats and opportunities that sit outside the project's authority and belong to someone higher up.

For opportunities, the mirror strategies:

- **Exploit**: make sure it happens, such as assigning the best engineer to secure an early finish bonus.
- **Share**: partner with someone better placed to capture it.
- **Enhance**: raise its probability or benefit.
- **Accept**: take it if it comes.

Every response needs an owner and a date, and is usually a task. A response with no owner is a hope.

## Monitor

Review the top risks weekly in the working group and the full log at least monthly. For each: has the probability or impact changed, is the response happening, has its trigger fired? Close risks that have passed. Watch for new ones after every change, gate and vendor update.

## Risk or issue?

A risk has not happened yet; an issue has. "The vendor might miss the delivery date" is a risk. "The vendor missed the delivery date" is an issue, managed now (see [[issues-and-escalation]]). When a risk occurs, close it and open an issue, so the log shows both what you foresaw and what you are dealing with.

## In Compass

Each project's RAID tab scores risks on probability and impact from 1 to 5. The score shows red from 15 and amber from 8, and a 5 × 5 heat grid counts open risks per cell; tap a cell to filter. The portfolio counts open risks and high risks (score 15 or more) per project. See [[raid-log]] for the fields.

## In practice

- Rewrite your three vaguest risks as cause, event, effect.
- Agree with the sponsor what impact 3 and impact 5 mean on your project, in days and dollars.
- Make sure every risk scoring 15 or more has an owner, a dated response and a task.
- Look for one opportunity worth exploiting and log it.
- Close or convert every risk that has already happened.

title: The RAID log
body:
A RAID log keeps four kinds of project uncertainty in one place: **risks**, **assumptions**, **issues** and **dependencies**. They belong together because they turn into each other. An assumption that proves false becomes an issue; a dependency that looks shaky is a risk; a risk that happens is an issue. One log, reviewed on a rhythm, stops those transitions from going unnoticed.

## The four types

**Risks**: things that might happen and would affect the project, for better or worse. "The customer's change freeze in December may push wave 4 into January."

**Assumptions**: things the plan treats as true without proof. "The customer provides rack space and power at every site." Each assumption needs an owner who will confirm it, and a date by which it must be confirmed. Unchecked assumptions are where many telecom projects quietly lose months.

**Issues**: problems happening now that need action. "Site 22's landlord has refused access for the fibre lateral." Issues get an owner, a response and a deadline, and sometimes an escalation (see [[issues-and-escalation]]).

**Dependencies**: things the project needs from outside its control, or that others need from it. "The ordering portal release from the IT team, needed before the first customer order." Name the person on the other side, not just their team.

Some organisations read the D as decisions instead. Compass keeps decisions in their own tab, so here D means dependencies.

## Fields worth keeping

| Field | Why it matters |
|---|---|
| Type | Risk, assumption, issue or dependency |
| Description | Specific enough to act on; for risks, cause, event and effect |
| Probability (risks) | 1–5 |
| Impact | 1–5, against agreed definitions |
| Score (risks) | Probability × impact, used to rank |
| Owner | One person who will act, not a team |
| Response | What is being done: the strategy and the concrete actions |
| Trigger | The sign that a risk is about to happen or needs a decision |
| Due date | When the response or confirmation is due |
| Status | Open or closed |

More fields, such as category, date raised, proximity or residual score, help on very large programmes. On most projects they mainly make the log slower to keep up to date, and an out-of-date log is worse than a short one.

## Review rhythm

- **Weekly**, in the working group: new items, everything scoring 15 or more, every open issue, assumptions due for confirmation this week, and dependencies due in the next two weeks. Ten to fifteen minutes.
- **Monthly**, or at each phase: the full log. Rescore, close what has passed, retire stale items, and look for gaps.
- **At each gate**: the log is part of the evidence. What is open, what is the exposure, and is it acceptable to go ahead?
- **After any change, incident or vendor update**: add what it raised.

The steering committee should see only the items that need its help, not the whole log.

## How Compass's RAID tab works

Every project has a RAID tab.

- **Adding**: choose the type, describe the item, and add it. Each row then holds owner, response, due date (and a trigger for risks) and an Open / Closed toggle; text fields save when you leave them.
- **Scoring**: a risk has probability and impact selects from 1 to 5 and a score chip, red at 15 or more and amber from 8 to 14. An issue has impact only.
- **Heat grid**: a 5 × 5 grid of open risks, impact across and probability up, with a count in each cell. Tap a cell to filter the list to it; tap again to clear.
- **Filters**: chips by type, and "Show closed" to include closed items.
- **Make a task**: turns an item into a task on the board with the item's text, so the response is tracked where you work.
- **From meetings**: when you accept a meeting review into a project, open questions and notes marked Risk or Issue land here with a "from meeting" chip.
- **Elsewhere**: the portfolio shows each project's open risks and high risks; the status report lists open risks by score, and the RAID log template exports all four types as tables.
- **Trash**: deleting moves an item to Trash, where it can be restored for 30 days.

## In practice

- Add an owner and a confirmation date to every assumption in your log.
- For each dependency, write the name of the person on the other side.
- Book a fifteen-minute RAID slot in this week's working group.
- Close or convert every risk that has already happened.
- Use "Make a task" for every open item scoring 15 or more that does not yet have one.

title: Procurement and contracts
body:
Much of what a telecom project delivers is bought: equipment, installation crews, carrier circuits, software licences, specialist engineers. The contract decides what you can insist on when things go wrong, so the PM needs to understand it well, even when procurement (approvisionnement) and legal own the process. At Bell, as in most large organisations, purchasing follows set policies and approval levels; this page covers the concepts, not any internal procedure.

## Asking the market: RFI, RFP, RFQ

The three requests answer different questions:

| Request | French | The question it asks | When to use it |
|---|---|---|---|
| RFI, request for information | Demande d'information (or de renseignements) | What exists, and who can do it? | Early, when you are still shaping the solution |
| RFP, request for proposal | Demande de propositions | How would you solve this, and at what price? | When the need is clear but the solution is open |
| RFQ, request for quotation | Demande de prix | What is your price for exactly this? | When the specification is fixed, for example a list of equipment |

A frequent sequence on a large deal is an RFI to shortlist, then an RFP to the shortlist. An RFQ suits commodities where price and delivery are the only real differences. Whatever the type, write the evaluation criteria and their weights before the responses arrive, so the choice can be explained later.

## What a statement of work holds

The statement of work (énoncé des travaux) is where the vendor's job is defined. Disputes almost always trace back to something it left vague. A solid one covers:

- **Background and objectives**: why the work exists.
- **Scope**: the deliverables and services, and an explicit list of what is excluded.
- **Location and access**: sites, hours, who arranges access, safety requirements.
- **Schedule**: milestones, lead times, and what happens when the customer or Bell causes a delay.
- **Roles**: what the vendor provides and what Bell or the customer provides (power, rack space, escorts, configurations).
- **Standards**: technical specifications, documentation formats, security and privacy requirements.
- **Acceptance criteria**: how each deliverable is checked and who signs.
- **Reporting and governance**: status cadence, meetings, escalation contacts.
- **Service levels and remedies**: where they apply (see [[vendor-management]]).
- **Pricing and payment**: tied to milestones or acceptance where possible.
- **Change process**: how scope changes are requested, priced and approved.

## Contract types: who carries the risk

| Type | French | How the vendor is paid | Who carries the cost risk | Fits when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Fixed price | Prix forfaitaire | An agreed amount for the defined scope | Mostly the vendor | Scope is clear and stable |
| Time and materials | Temps et matériel | Hours at agreed rates, plus materials | Mostly the buyer | Scope is unclear or evolving, or for short expert help |
| Cost-plus | Prix coûtant majoré | Actual costs plus a fee, fixed or a percentage | Mostly the buyer | Novel or high-uncertainty work where a fixed price would be padded |

The trade-offs follow from the risk. A fixed price looks safe but pushes the vendor to read the scope narrowly and to charge for every change, so the statement of work has to be precise. Time and materials is flexible but needs a cap (a "not to exceed" amount) and close tracking of hours. Cost-plus needs audit rights and trust. Variants such as unit pricing (per site, per circuit) are common in rollouts and combine a fixed rate with a variable quantity.

## Acceptance criteria

Acceptance (acceptation) is the moment the buyer agrees the deliverable meets the contract, and often when payment is due. Good criteria are:

- **Measurable**: "all ports pass the agreed test plan, results attached", not "working to the customer's satisfaction".
- **Agreed upfront**, in the statement of work, not negotiated at delivery.
- **Owned**: who tests, who signs, and within how many days, with what happens if nobody signs.
- **Staged** where it helps: per site or per wave, so payment and problems do not pile up at the end.

Keep vendor and customer acceptance in step. If the vendor's work is finally accepted long before the customer accepts the service, defects found in between are Bell's to absorb; a held-back final payment or a warranty period covers the gap.

## In Compass

Keep the statement of work and the signed contract as project documents, log contract risks and vendor dependencies in the RAID log, and record award and acceptance decisions in Decisions.

## In practice

- Read the statement of work for your main vendor and list every deliverable without a measurable acceptance criterion.
- Write down the contract type and what that means for who pays when scope changes.
- Find the change clause and confirm how a change is priced and approved.
- Check what covers defects found between vendor acceptance and the customer's acceptance: a holdback, a warranty, or nothing.
- Agree with procurement the evaluation criteria for your next request before it goes out.

title: Quality management
body:
On a telecom project, poor quality rarely shows up on delivery day. It shows up three weeks after go-live, when a site drops every afternoon, the as-built records do not match what is in the rack, or the customer's first invoice is wrong. Quality management (gestion de la qualité) is about deciding in advance what "good" means for each deliverable, building the work so it gets there, and checking before the customer finds out.

## Quality planning: decide what good means

Before the work starts, for each major deliverable, answer:

- **Which standards apply?** The customer's requirements, the contract, Bell's engineering and security standards, vendor specifications, regulations.
- **How will we know it meets them?** Tests, inspections, reviews, measurements, with pass and fail thresholds.
- **Who checks, and when?** Ideally someone other than the person who did the work, and early enough to fix cheaply.
- **What records prove it?** Test results, signed checklists, photos of the install, configuration backups.

Write this as a short quality plan, or a section in the project plan. For an SD-WAN rollout it might list the site acceptance test (link up, failover, performance thresholds, monitoring visible in the operations tools), the documentation required per site, and who signs.

## Assurance vs control

The two are often confused, because both involve checking. They check different things.

**Quality assurance** (assurance qualité) looks at the way the work is done. Its question is: if we keep working like this, will the results be right? Examples: reviewing the method of procedure before the first cutover; checking that the install vendor's technicians are certified and use the agreed checklist; auditing whether test results are actually recorded; running a lessons session after the pilot sites. It is preventive, and it happens before and during the work.

**Quality control** (contrôle de la qualité) looks at the results. Its question is: does this deliverable meet its criteria? Examples: running the site acceptance test; inspecting cabling and labelling; reviewing the configuration against the design; sampling as-built records. It finds defects, so they can be fixed and their causes fed back to assurance.

A project that does only control finds the same defect at site after site. A project that does only assurance has good processes and no proof that the outputs work. You need both, and the link between them: every recurring defect found by control should change a process.

## Acceptance

Acceptance is the formal step where the person entitled to say "yes, this meets what we agreed" says it, in writing. Make it work by:

- agreeing the criteria in the statement of work or the charter, before delivery (see [[procurement-and-contracts]]);
- accepting in stages, such as per site or per wave, rather than all at the end;
- naming who signs, and how long they have, and what happens if nobody responds;
- recording any accepted deviation or punch-list item, with an owner and a date.

On customer projects, the customer's acceptance often triggers billing and the start of the service term, so it deserves as much planning as the cutover itself.

## Definition of done

In agile workstreams, the definition of done (définition de « terminé ») is the team's shared checklist that every backlog item must pass before it counts as finished. It is a quality commitment, not a wish list. For a portal or integration team it might include: code reviewed, automated tests passing, tested end to end with ordering and billing in a test environment, security scan clean, documentation updated, demo accepted by the product owner.

The same idea works outside software. A "done" checklist for a site install could include: equipment installed and labelled, tests passed and attached, as-built uploaded, customer contact signed, monitoring confirmed by operations. A task is only moved to done on the board when every line is true. When teams argue about whether something is done, the checklist is missing or unclear.

## In Compass

Write the acceptance criteria into the project's success criteria field and the definition of done into each relevant task's notes. Log quality risks and recurring defects in the RAID log, and the lessons they teach in the Lessons tab.

## In practice

- Write or update the acceptance test for your next deliverable, with pass and fail thresholds.
- Pick one assurance check, such as a method of procedure review, and schedule it before the next cutover.
- Draft a "done" checklist for your most repeated task, such as a site install, and agree it with the vendor.
- Look at the last five defects and ask which process would have prevented them.
- Confirm who signs customer acceptance, and how long they have.

title: Vendor management
body:
Once the contract is signed, the vendor becomes part of your delivery team without being under your authority. You cannot assign their people or set their priorities; you can only use the contract, the relationship and the information you share. Vendor management (gestion des fournisseurs) is the work of turning a signed agreement into dependable delivery, and of noticing early when it is not happening.

## Kick-off

Hold a proper kick-off with each significant vendor, separate from the customer kick-off. Cover:

- **The goal and the customer**: what the project is for, what matters to the customer, what would embarrass everyone.
- **The contract in plain terms**: scope, exclusions, milestones, acceptance, service levels, the change process. Read it together; their delivery team may never have seen it.
- **People**: named contacts on both sides, who decides what, and the escalation path with names (see [[issues-and-escalation]]).
- **Ways of working**: status format and timing, meeting rhythm, tools, how site access and logistics are arranged, safety and security rules.
- **Known risks and dependencies**, in both directions: what you need from them, and what they need from Bell and the customer.

Send a summary afterwards and treat it as the start of the record.

## Cadence

- **Weekly** working session with the vendor's PM: progress against the plan, the next two weeks, blockers, risks, actions from both sides.
- **Monthly** or quarterly service review with the vendor's account manager: the scorecard, trends, commercial matters, improvement actions.
- **Daily** during intense periods such as install waves or cutovers.

Ask for status in a format you can compare week to week, ideally against the same milestones you report to your own sponsor.

## Service levels

Service level agreements (ententes de niveau de service, ENS) turn expectations into measurable commitments: equipment delivered within so many days of order, installs completed within the booked window, defects fixed within a time based on severity, reports delivered by a day each month. Good SLAs measure what the customer actually feels, and come with a clear measurement method and a remedy, such as service credits, an improvement plan, or, ultimately, the right to terminate.

Know which SLAs are in your vendor's contract and which are in Bell's contract with the customer. Gaps between the two, such as a vendor fix time longer than the time Bell promised the customer, are risks for the RAID log.

## Scorecards

A short scorecard (fiche d'évaluation) reviewed monthly keeps the conversation factual. Pick five to eight measures:

| Area | Example measure |
|---|---|
| Schedule | Milestones met on the agreed date, percentage |
| Quality | Sites passing acceptance at the first visit |
| Responsiveness | Time to answer escalations |
| Documentation | As-built records delivered with each site |
| Safety and compliance | Incidents, missed access rules |
| Commercial | Invoices accurate first time |
| Collaboration | Risks raised early by the vendor |

Show the trend, not only the month. Share the scorecard with the vendor before the review, so the meeting is about causes and actions, not about disputing the numbers.

## Handling slippage

When a vendor starts missing dates:

1. **Notice early.** Compare their forecasts with what actually happened, and challenge an unchanged forecast after a missed week.
2. **Understand the cause.** Capacity, supply, a dependency on Bell or the customer, or a real misunderstanding of scope? Some causes are yours to fix.
3. **Ask for a recovery plan** in writing, with dates, resources and checkpoints. Agree how you will track it, often more often than usual.
4. **Protect the critical path.** Resequence work, ask for a second crew, or source parts elsewhere, within the contract's terms.
5. **Record it.** Missed dates, recovery commitments and their outcomes, for the scorecard and for any later commercial discussion.

## Escalating with a vendor

Follow the contract's path, step by step: their PM, then their account or delivery manager, then a named executive. Warn your counterpart before you go above them. Bring facts, the impact, and a clear ask. Involve Bell procurement or vendor management before any commercial remedy such as withholding payment or invoking penalties; those are their tools, and using them badly damages a relationship you may need for years. A firm, fair, well-documented escalation often earns more respect from a vendor than months of tolerance.

## In Compass

Put each vendor commitment on the board as a task in the Waiting on column with the vendor's name, so waiting-on nudges, the weekly review and overdue alerts catch it. Log vendor risks and dependencies in the RAID log, and record recovery commitments and remedies in Decisions.

## In practice

- Read your main vendor's SLAs next to the customer's, and log any gap as a risk.
- Draft a six-line scorecard and send it to the vendor before your next review.
- Check that every open vendor action is on the board under Waiting on, with a due date.
- Write down the vendor's escalation path with names and phone numbers.
- Ask for a written recovery plan on any milestone the vendor has already missed.

title: Exception reports
body:
A status report tells the sponsor where the project stands. An exception report (rapport d'exception) tells them something different: the project is about to leave the space it was allowed to operate in, and the PM no longer has the authority to fix it alone. It comes from PRINCE2's idea of management by exception (see [[prince2-processes]]), and it is useful far beyond PRINCE2 projects, because it turns a bad surprise into a structured decision.

## When to write one

Write it when a tolerance is **forecast** to break, not when it has already broken. The point is to give the decision makers time and options while both still exist.

Typical triggers, using the tolerances agreed at the start (see [[change-control]]):

- A committed milestone is forecast to slip beyond its tolerance, such as more than five working days on a customer go-live.
- The cost forecast exceeds the budget tolerance, for example an estimate at completion more than 5% over.
- A deliverable will not meet agreed scope or quality, such as a feature the contract requires that the vendor cannot deliver.
- A key benefit in the business case is no longer achievable.
- A risk with a score at or above the agreed threshold becomes very likely and its response has failed.

If you find yourself wondering whether a situation deserves an exception report, it usually deserves at least a phone call to the sponsor today, followed by the report.

An exception report is not a substitute for the escalation of an urgent issue that needs action within hours (see [[issues-and-escalation]]). It is for decisions about the plan.

## The sections

1. **Situation**: the project, its current RAG and the one-line reason. Which tolerance is forecast to break, and by how much.
2. **Cause**: what happened, in facts. Separate the trigger (the vendor missed the delivery) from any underlying cause (single-source supply with no buffer).
3. **Consequences**: what happens if nothing changes, for milestones, cost, the customer, the business case, other projects. Include the overdue tasks and late milestones that already show the problem.
4. **Options**: usually three, each with its trade-offs.
5. **Recommendation**: which option, why, and what decision is needed by when.
6. **Risks and issues**: the open items that bear on the decision.

Once a decision is made, the project often needs an exception plan (plan d'exception): a revised plan for the rest of the stage or phase, which becomes the new baseline once approved.

## Options with trade-offs

The options are the heart of the report. A sponsor given one option is being asked to rubber-stamp; one given no options is being handed your problem. Good options:

- **Are genuinely different**, not the same option at three price points.
- **Include "do nothing" or "accept the slip"** when it is realistic, so its cost is visible.
- **State the cost of each in the same terms**: dates, dollars, scope, risk, customer impact.
- **Name what each makes worse**, not only what it fixes.

Example, a managed network rollout where the vendor's equipment for wave 3 is six weeks late:

| Option | Schedule | Cost | Risk and customer impact |
|---|---|---|---|
| A. Accept the delay | Wave 3 go-live moves six weeks | No extra cost now; possible contract credit | Customer escalation likely; crews idle |
| B. Source equipment from a second distributor | Delay cut to two weeks | Higher unit price, roughly $40,000 more | New supplier untested; extra configuration checks needed |
| C. Resequence: bring wave 4 sites forward | Overall end date holds | Small replanning cost | Wave 4 sites need early readiness checks; customer must agree to the new order |

Recommendation: C, with B as a fallback if the customer cannot ready wave 4 sites by the 15th; decision needed from the steering committee by Friday to keep the install crews booked.

## Writing it

Keep it to two pages at most, with the options table on the first. Send it before the meeting where it will be decided, and walk the sponsor through it beforehand so they can support the recommendation. Record the decision and its conditions in the decision log, update the plan, and tell the team and the customer what changed.

## In Compass

The exception report template fills the situation from the project's RAG and reason, lists overdue tasks and late milestones under Consequences, and adds the open risks and issues; Cause and Options start blank for you to write. On a project that allows cloud AI, the copilot's "Exception report" preset drafts the cause, impact, options and recommendation for you to check. Record the outcome in Decisions and any approved changes in the Changes tab.

## In practice

- Check each project's forecast against its tolerances and list any that will break within a month.
- For the closest one, draft three genuinely different options with their costs.
- Call the sponsor before sending any exception report.
- After the decision, re-baseline the plan and log the decision with its conditions.

title: Status reporting and RAG
body:
A status report (rapport d'état) has one job: to let its readers decide whether they need to do anything. Most reports fail at it by describing activity instead of position. "Team worked on site surveys" is activity. "Surveys are 18 of 25 done, two sites blocked on landlord access, wave 2 still on track for the 30th" is position. Write for the second.

## RAG that means something

Red, amber, green is useful only when everyone reads the colours the same way. Without definitions, green means "I'd rather not discuss it" and red appears only when it is too late. Agree thresholds with the sponsor at the start and print them on the report.

An example set, tied to the project's tolerances:

| RAG | Schedule | Cost | Scope and quality | What it asks of the reader |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Green** | Every committed milestone forecast on time or up to 5 working days late | Forecast no more than 5% over budget | As agreed | Nothing |
| **Amber** | A committed milestone forecast 6 to 15 working days late, with a recovery plan the team can carry out | Forecast more than 5% and up to 10% over | A change is pending, or a quality problem is being fixed | Awareness; maybe a small decision |
| **Red** | A committed milestone forecast more than 15 days late, or no credible recovery plan | Forecast more than 10% over | A deliverable will not meet the agreed scope or quality | Action or a decision from the sponsor or steering committee |

The numbers above are illustrations; set yours to match the project's tolerances. Three rules keep RAG honest:

- **Rate the forecast, not the past.** A project that was late but has a credible plan to recover can be amber. One that is on time today but will miss next month's milestone is already amber or red.
- **Always give the reason** in one line next to the colour.
- **Show the trend**: better, same or worse since last time. Amber getting worse needs more attention than a steady amber.

Never go from green straight to red if you could have seen it coming. That is the one thing executives remember.

## The sections of a status report

1. **Overall status**: RAG, reason and the reporting period.
2. **Executive summary**: three to five sentences. Where we are, what changed, what we need.
3. **Progress**: what was finished this period, as results.
4. **Next steps**: what is due in the next two weeks.
5. **Milestones**: name, planned date, forecast or actual, and a state such as done, late, due this period or upcoming.
6. **Risks and issues**: the top few only, with owner and response.
7. **Decisions needed**: what, from whom, by when.
8. **Decisions made**: so the record is complete.

Optional, depending on the audience: budget (planned, spent, forecast), change requests, earned value (see [[earned-value]]).

## Writing for executives

- **Lead with the ask.** If you need a decision, put it in the first two lines, not on page three.
- **One page.** Details go in an appendix or the working group.
- **Numbers over adjectives.** "Three days late" rather than "slightly delayed".
- **No surprises.** Anything red should have been raised by phone before the report goes out.
- **Same format every time**, so readers know where to look and can compare weeks.
- **Plain language, no internal jargon** about tools and ticket numbers. Use the customer's name for things.
- **In the reader's language.** For French-speaking executives, a French report reads as respect, not a courtesy.

## In Compass

Set the project's RAG and its reason on the project page; the portfolio shows them with % done, the next milestone, open and high risks, and pending changes for every active project. The Report tab builds the status report from the project's own data for a period (this week, the last two weeks, this month or custom dates), with the sections above, and exports it to Word, Markdown or PDF. On a project that allows cloud AI, "Write the summary with the copilot" drafts the executive summary; otherwise the summary is the progress line, which you can edit in Word.

## In practice

- Write RAG thresholds for your project and get the sponsor to agree them by email.
- Rewrite last week's progress section as results, with numbers.
- Put the decisions you need in the first two lines of your next report.
- Add the trend (better, same or worse) to your next report, and to the RAG reason in Compass.
- Check that every red or amber item in the report has an owner and a date.

title: Closing a project
body:
Projects rarely end cleanly. The last sites go live, the team drifts to new work, a few defects linger, the vendor's final invoice arrives months later, and nobody is quite sure whether the project is still open. Closing on purpose (clôture du projet) protects the customer, the budget and your reputation, and it frees people properly for what comes next. On most projects it takes two to four weeks of deliberate work.

## Acceptance

Closing starts with confirming the project delivered what was agreed:

- **Customer acceptance**: the customer signs that the service or deliverables meet the acceptance criteria. Get it in writing, referencing the contract or statement of work. On B2B work this often starts billing and the service term, so the account team needs the date.
- **Internal acceptance**: the sponsor confirms the objectives in the charter are met, or records which are not and why.
- **Open items**: anything accepted with reservations goes on a punch list with an owner, a date and a home after the project ends.

If acceptance is stalling, find out why. Usually there is a real defect, or a missing document, or the customer is using acceptance as leverage on an unrelated issue. Each needs a different answer.

## Handover to operations

The service must keep running after the project team leaves. A good handover (transfert à l'exploitation) means operations accepts responsibility knowingly, not by default:

- **Documentation**: as-built records, network diagrams, configurations, IP plans, circuit IDs, vendor contacts, support contracts and their expiry dates.
- **Inventory and systems**: every site, device and circuit recorded correctly in the inventory, monitoring and billing systems. Mismatches here become incidents and billing disputes for years.
- **Support model**: who the customer calls, escalation paths, SLAs, maintenance windows, warranty terms.
- **Known issues**: open defects and workarounds, transferred formally with owners.
- **Training and early support**: a period, often two to four weeks, where the project team backs up operations for questions.

Ask operations to sign the handover. This is often the evidence for the final gate, Gate 5 in [[project-lifecycle]].

## Administrative closure

The paperwork nobody enjoys and everybody needs:

- **Contracts**: confirm every vendor deliverable is accepted, final invoices received and paid, holdbacks released or claimed, and purchase orders closed.
- **Finance**: reconcile the budget, close cost codes so no more charges land on the project, and record the final cost against the baseline.
- **Records**: archive the project documents where the organisation keeps them, with decisions, approvals and acceptance signatures easy to find.
- **People**: release team members formally, tell their managers, and give feedback on their contribution.
- **Benefits**: hand the business case's benefits to the person who will measure them after the project, with the measures and dates.
- **Lessons**: hold the closing lessons session (see [[lessons-learned]]).

## Celebrating

Mark the end. A team lunch, a short note from the sponsor naming individuals and what they did, a message to the customer's team thanking them. It costs little and people remember it at the start of the next project, when you need them again. Thank the vendor's people too; they were part of the team. Recognition works best when it is specific: "the weekend cutover went cleanly because Marc rebuilt the rollback plan on Friday" lands far better than "thanks, everyone".

## In Compass

Tick the final milestones done, record acceptance and handover sign-offs in Decisions, close or transfer the open RAID items, and capture lessons in the Lessons tab. The lessons learned template builds a closing document from the project. Then set the project's status to closed: it leaves the portfolio's active list and moves under "Closed".

## In practice

- Write the closing checklist for your nearest project end: acceptance, handover, contracts, finance, people, lessons.
- Ask operations what they need in the handover pack, before you build it.
- Check with finance which cost codes are still open on finished projects.
- Book the lessons session and the team celebration now, before people move on.
- Draft the thank-you note to the team, naming what each person did.

title: Lessons learned
body:
Most organisations hold a lessons learned session at the end of a project, write a document, file it, and never open it again. The next project then repeats the same mistakes with the same vendor. Lessons learned (leçons apprises in Québec; retour d'expérience, or REX, is more common in France) are only worth the effort if they are collected while memories are fresh, written so someone else can act on them, and stored where the next PM will actually find them.

## Collect during the project, not only at the end

By the closing session, people remember the last month and the most dramatic week. The small, useful lessons from the design phase are gone, and half the team has moved on. Collect as you go:

- **At each gate or phase end**: fifteen minutes in the working group on "what should we keep, and what should we change for the next phase?".
- **After any significant event**: a failed cutover, a vendor escalation, a pilot. A short review within a week, while the details are clear and people are still there.
- **In retrospectives** for agile workstreams, where the habit already exists. Pull the lessons that matter beyond the team into the project's list.
- **When you notice one**: a two-line note the moment something surprises you. It takes thirty seconds.

The closing session then becomes a review of a list that already exists, plus the overall view: did the project meet its objectives, and what would we do differently from the start?

## Running a session that people are honest in

- Agree up front that it is about the system, not about blame. People will not tell you what went wrong if they expect to be named for it.
- Invite the vendor and the customer's team for at least part of it; their view is the one you cannot get alone.
- Use a simple structure: what went well, what did not, what we would do differently. Spend most of the time on the third.
- Start from facts: the timeline, the milestones, the issues log. Memory alone favours the dramatic.

## A format that can be reused

A lesson that says "communication could have been better" teaches nothing. Write each one so a PM who was not there can act on it:

| Part | Example |
|---|---|
| Context | Multi-site SD-WAN rollout, 60 sites, two install vendors |
| What happened | Twelve sites failed first-visit installs because the customer's site contacts had not confirmed rack space and power |
| Effect | Each failed visit cost a second truck roll and about a week; wave 2 slipped three weeks |
| Lesson | Treat site readiness as a deliverable owned by the customer, with a signed checklist per site, not an assumption |
| Action for next time | Add a site readiness checklist and a confirmation call 10 days before each install to the standard plan |
| Category | Site readiness |

The category matters more than it seems. It is what lets someone searching later find all the lessons about vendors, site readiness, cutovers or billing, regardless of which project they came from. Keep a short, stable set of categories rather than inventing a new one each time.

Turn each important lesson into a change somewhere: a checklist, a template, a standard risk, a contract clause. A lesson that changes nothing has only been recorded, not learned.

## Making them findable in Compass

Each project has a Lessons tab: add a lesson with its text and a category, and edit it in place at any time during the project, not only at the end. Write the lesson in the format above, condensed into the text.

- **Lessons from personal projects** are searchable in the library, under Lessons, alongside these pages.
- **Lessons from work projects** stay inside their project and are encrypted with the rest of its work data, so they do not appear in the library.
- **The copilot** reads a project's lessons when it answers questions about that project, as part of the project's context.
- **The lessons learned template** builds a closing document from the project: a project summary, what went well, what to improve, the lessons table with categories, and actions for next time.

Before starting a new project, search the library for the relevant category and read what your past self wrote.

## In practice

- Add three lessons from your current project to its Lessons tab this week, each with a category.
- Agree a list of six to ten categories and use only those.
- Add a fifteen-minute lessons slot to the agenda of the next phase-end or gate meeting.
- Pick one lesson from a past project and turn it into a change in your standard plan or checklist.
- Before your next project kick-off, search for lessons in its main category.

title: Template guide: change request
body:
The change request template turns one entry on the project's Changes tab into a document an approver can read, sign and file. You generate it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab, as Word, Markdown or PDF. When the project has several change requests, Compass asks which one; with none chosen it takes the newest pending request, and with none at all it gives you the same form with blank fields to fill in by hand. Writing the request well is most of the work of change control: a clear request gets a quick decision, a vague one gets sent back. The process around it, from tolerances to the change board, is in [[change-control]].

## Request

Five fields: project, title, approver, decision and date. All but the project name come from the change on the Changes tab.

- **Title**: one line that says what would change, not why. "Add six sites to wave 3" is a title; "Customer request" is not.
- **Approver**: the person or body with authority for a change of this size, as set in the charter or your governance. A change that moves a contract date or the budget usually needs the sponsor, and sometimes the customer.
- **Decision and date**: pending until someone decides. When you mark the change approved or rejected, Compass sets the decision date; set it back to pending and the date clears.
- **Mistakes**: the PM named as approver of a change to their own budget; a decision recorded with no date.

## Description

The change's description from the Changes tab.

- **Good**: what is being asked, by whom, and why now, in a few sentences. Say what happens if it is not approved, because "no" is always an option and the approver needs to know its cost too.
- **Mistakes**: a description that is really a solution ("buy more routers") with no statement of the need; jargon only the delivery team understands.
- **Example**: "The customer has opened six new branch offices since the contract was signed and asks for them to join wave 3 rather than a later project. Without the change, the six sites stay on separate internet links with no central management until a new order is placed."

## Impact

Three fields: scope, time and cost, from the change's three impact fields.

- **Scope**: what is added, removed or altered, including deliverables nobody mentioned in the request: surveys, documentation, operations handover, billing setup.
- **Time**: the effect on milestones, in dates, not adjectives. Say whether the change touches the critical path.
- **Cost**: one-time and recurring, internal and vendor. Note who pays: the customer through a contract amendment, or the project's contingency.
- **Good**: numbers with their source ("vendor quote 14 Jan"), and an honest range when the estimate is rough.
- **Mistakes**: "minimal impact"; a time impact without checking the vendor's lead times; forgetting the effect on risk, which you can add as a line under the three fields.
- **Example**: scope, six extra surveys, installs and acceptances; time, wave 3 ends 2 weeks later, final milestone unchanged; cost, $54,000 one-time, recovered through a contract amendment.

## Recommendation

Left blank: this is the PM's view, and Compass does not write it for you.

- **Good**: approve, reject or defer, with one or two reasons and any condition ("approve, provided the amendment is signed before equipment is ordered"). If you recommend rejecting, offer a route: a later phase or a separate order.
- **Mistakes**: no recommendation, which hands your judgement to the approver; a recommendation that ignores the impact you just described.

## After the decision

Record the outcome on the Changes tab so the decision and its date are set, and log it in the Decisions tab with any conditions. Then update what the change touched: milestones, tasks, the budget fields and the RAID log. Pending requests appear in the status report under Decisions needed, so a request left pending after a verbal yes keeps asking for a decision that was already made.

## In practice

- Open the Changes tab and check every pending request has an approver.
- Rewrite one request's title so it states the change in a single line.
- Fill in time impact as dates on your next request, not "a few weeks".
- Write a recommendation before you send the document.
- Close out any change decided verbally but still pending.
