- [[procurement-and-contracts]]
- [[template-status-report]]
- [[meetings-and-governance]]

title: Template guide: exception report
body:
The exception report template gives you the frame for the document you write when a tolerance is forecast to break. Compass fills the parts that are facts already on the project: the situation, the overdue work and late milestones, and the open risks and issues. It leaves the parts that need your judgement blank: the cause, the options and, unless you have a drafted summary, the recommendation. You generate it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab, as Word, Markdown or PDF, and finish it in Word. When to write one, and how the decision that follows works, is in [[exception-reports]].

## Situation

Three fields: project, RAG and its reason, from the project page.

- **Good**: by the time you write an exception report the RAG is usually red, and the reason names the tolerance and the size of the forecast breach: "Red: final cutover forecast 18 working days late against a tolerance of 10."
- **Mistakes**: generating the report while the RAG still says green, which tells the sponsor the project page is out of date; a reason that blames without informing ("vendor issues").
- **Tip**: update the RAG and reason first, then generate.

## Cause

Left blank. Write what happened in facts, and separate the trigger from the underlying cause.

- **Good**: "Trigger: the router distributor cut our wave 3 allocation by 40%. Underlying cause: a single supply source with no buffer stock, a risk logged in October with a response that was never carried out."
- **Mistakes**: a cause that is really a symptom ("cutovers delayed"); naming people instead of the conditions that let it happen.

## Consequences

Compass lists the project's overdue tasks and late milestones, the evidence already visible in the plan.

- **Good**: add, in a few lines, what happens if nothing changes: the forecast dates, the cost, the customer's position, the effect on the business case and on other projects. The lists support the story; they do not tell it.
- **Mistakes**: pasting the lists with no explanation; leaving out the consequence the sponsor cares most about, which is often the customer relationship or a contractual penalty.

## Options

Left blank, with space for options A, B and C and their trade-offs. This is the heart of the report.

- **Good**: options that are genuinely different, each stated in the same terms: dates, cost, scope, risk and customer impact. Include "accept the slip" when it is realistic, so its cost is visible next to the others.
- **Mistakes**: one real option and two straw men; options without numbers; an option that needs someone else's approval without saying whose.

For a router shortage on a 60-site rollout, the three might be:

- A: pay for air freight from a second distributor; +$38,000, recovers 12 of the 18 days.
- B: re-sequence, cutting over the 20 sites with equipment in hand first; no cost, 10 days late, more night work.
- C: accept the slip and negotiate the date with the customer; no cost, 18 days late, contract penalty to be discussed.

On a project that allows cloud AI, the copilot's "Exception report" preset can draft causes, options with trade-offs and a recommendation for you to check and rewrite.

## Recommendation

If you had the copilot write the summary on the Report tab, Compass places that text here as a starting point; otherwise the section is blank. Either way, rewrite it as a recommendation.

- **Good**: which option, why, and the decision you need from whom by when: "Recommend B, with A held in reserve. Decision needed from the sponsor by Thursday to book night crews."
- **Mistakes**: no deadline, so the decision drifts; a recommendation that is not one of the options.

## Risks and issues

Two tables from the RAID tab: open risks, highest score first, and open issues.

- **Good**: trim them to the items that bear on the decision, and add any new risk each option creates, such as crew fatigue under option B.
- **Mistakes**: sending forty rows that bury the two that matter.

## After the decision

Log the decision and its conditions in the Decisions tab, create tasks for the actions, adjust milestones and the RAG, and raise a change request if scope, time or cost tolerances move.

## In practice

- Log the agreed tolerances for the current stage in the Decisions tab, so a breach can be measured against them.
- If a tolerance is forecast to break, update the RAG and generate the report today.
- Write three options with numbers before you choose one.
- Put the decision deadline in the first line of the recommendation.
- After the decision, raise the change request the same day.

- [[template-status-report]]

title: Template guide: lessons learned
body:
The lessons learned template builds a closing document (leçons apprises) from the project's Lessons tab and its record, and leaves the reflective parts for you to write with the team. You generate it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab, as Word, Markdown or PDF. This page also explains how to make your own Word template, so Compass can fill a document in your organisation's format. How to collect lessons during the project is in [[lessons-learned]].

## Project summary

Key facts from the project record, such as the sponsor, dates and budget.

- **Good**: check the planned and spent budget and the end date are final before generating, so the summary states what really happened.
- **Mistake**: closing the document with the original end date when the project finished two months later.

## What went well

Left blank. Fill it in at the closing session.

- **Good**: specific practices worth repeating, with why they worked: "Confirmation calls ten days before each install cut failed visits from twelve in wave 1 to one in wave 3."
- **Mistake**: compliments instead of practices ("great team spirit").

## What to improve

Left blank.

- **Good**: conditions, not culprits, each tied to an effect you can measure.
- **Mistake**: a list so long that nothing on it will be acted on. Keep the five that cost the most.

## Lessons

A table of every lesson on the Lessons tab, with its category.

- **Good**: lessons written so a PM who was not there can act on them, and a small, stable set of categories, so the next project can find them.
- **Mistake**: adding all the lessons on the last day; most of the useful ones are forgotten by then.

## Actions for next time

Left blank.

- **Good**: each important lesson turned into a change with an owner: a checklist item, a standard risk, a contract clause.
- **Mistake**: actions with no owner, which means the lesson was recorded but not learned.

## Making your own Word template

When your organisation has a standard format, you can upload a `.docx` that contains placeholders in double braces, and Compass fills it with the project's data.

1. In Word, write the document as usual and type each placeholder where its value should go, for example `{{project.name}}`.
2. Upload it on the project's Documents tab and turn on "Use as template". Compass lists the placeholders it found; check each one is spelled as below, because an unknown name is filled with nothing.
3. On the Report tab, under your templates, choose Fill. Compass fills it on your device with the data for the report's current period and downloads a Word file. If the template is broken, for example a loop that is never closed, Compass shows a message starting "Template problem".

Single values Compass fills:

| Group | Placeholders |
|---|---|
| Project | `project.` followed by name, kind, status, phase, rag, rag_label, rag_reason, sponsor, start_at, end_at, objectives, scope_in, scope_out, success_criteria, budget_planned, budget_spent, budget_left, pct_done |
| Status | `status.headline`, `status.progress`, `status.next_steps`, `ai.summary` |
| Period | `range.label`, `range.from`, `range.to`, `generated_at` |

Lists Compass fills. Each one offers `.table` (rows as text separated by vertical bars, with a header line), `.list` (bullet lines), `.count`, and `.rows` for a loop over these fields:

| List | Fields in each row |
|---|---|
| `milestones` | name, due_at, done_at, gate, state |
| `tasks.done` | title, done_at |
| `tasks.open` | title, status, due_at, waiting_on |
| `tasks.overdue` | title, due_at, days_late |
| `tasks.next` | title, due_at |
| `risks` | text, probability, impact, score, owner, response, trigger |
| `issues` | text, impact, owner, response |
| `assumptions` | text |
| `dependencies` | text, owner |
| `changes` | title, decision, impact_scope, impact_time, impact_cost, approver, decided_at |
| `decisions` | decided_at, text |
| `decisions_needed` | title |
| `lessons` | text, category |
| `meetings` | title, date, summary |

A loop opens with `#` and closes with `/`. Inside it, use the row's field names alone:

```
{{#lessons.rows}}{{category}}: {{text}}{{/lessons.rows}}
```

For a real Word table, build one row with a field in each cell, and put the opening tag in the first cell and the closing tag in the last cell; the row repeats once per item. `ai.summary` is filled only after you have had the copilot write the summary on the Report tab.

## In practice

- Add your project's lessons to the Lessons tab now, with categories, so the table is ready at closing.
- Generate the document before the closing session and bring it as the agenda.
- Turn the top three lessons into actions, each with an owner.
- Rebuild your team's usual closing template in Word with placeholders and fill it from one project.

title: Template guide: project charter
body:
The charter template turns what you have already typed on a project into a document a sponsor can read and sign. Compass builds it on your device from the project's Overview fields, its milestones and its RAID tab, and you download it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab as Word, Markdown or PDF. The generator copies what is there and adds nothing, so a vague field becomes a vague charter (charte de projet). This guide goes through the document section by section: what Compass puts in it, what good looks like, and the mistakes to avoid. For why the charter matters and how it differs from the business case, see [[charter-and-business-case]].

## Summary

Compass fills six fields from the project record: project name, sponsor, phase, start, end and the planned budget.

- **Good**: the sponsor (commanditaire) is one named person who can stop the project; the phase says where you are in the life cycle; the dates are the ones you will be held to; the budget says what it covers.
- **Mistakes**: a department as sponsor ("Enterprise Sales"); an end date that does not match the last milestone; a blank budget because "finance has it".
- **Example**: sponsor, director of enterprise network delivery; phase, Planning; 2026-11-02 to 2027-04-30; $480,000 one-time, covering internal labour and vendor installation, not the customer's monthly service fees.

## Objectives

Taken from the Objectives field on the Overview.

- **Good**: three to five outcomes, each with a measure and a date, each traceable to a benefit in the business case.
- **Mistakes**: activities instead of results ("deploy SD-WAN"), or a list of fifteen items that nobody can rank.
- **Example**: "All 38 branch sites carried on the managed SD-WAN service by 30 April, with the old MPLS circuits disconnected and their billing stopped within 30 days of each cutover."

## Scope

Two parts, from the In scope and Out of scope fields.

- **Good**: in scope names deliverables, not tasks. Out of scope names the things someone will plausibly ask for later, which is what makes it useful in an argument six months from now.
- **Mistakes**: an empty out-of-scope list; an in-scope list that repeats the objectives.
- **Example**: in, site surveys, router install and configuration, ten night cutover windows, two weeks of post-cutover support. Out, LAN cabling inside the customer's buildings, Wi-Fi redesign, rewriting firewall rules beyond the agreed standard policy.

## Success criteria

From the Success criteria field. These are how the sponsor will judge the whole project at closure; acceptance criteria for single deliverables belong in the contract or the quality plan (see [[quality-management]]).

- **Good**: measurable, with someone named to measure them, and a date when they can be measured.
- **Mistakes**: "customer satisfied"; criteria that only become measurable a year after closure, with nobody assigned to check.
- **Example**: 95% of sites cut over in their first planned window; no Severity 1 incident caused by the migration during the support period; final cost within 5% of budget.

## Milestones

A table of the project's milestones with their dates.

- **Good**: five to ten summary milestones, each an event that is either met or not. Include the gates: in Compass, mark a gate milestone so it shows the ◆ marker, and record each gate's outcome in the Decisions tab.
- **Mistakes**: forty rows copied from a vendor's schedule; milestones that are really ongoing activities ("testing").
- **Example**: design approved; pilot of five sites live; Gate 3, commit to build; waves 2 to 4 live; old circuits disconnected; closure.

## Key risks

The five highest-scoring open risks from the RAID tab, with probability, impact, score, owner and response.

- **Good**: each risk names a cause, an event and an effect; each has one owner and a response that is already under way.
- **Mistakes**: generic risks ("resources may be unavailable"); issues that have already happened listed as risks; responses that say "monitor".
- **Example**: "Building landlords control after-hours access, so a landlord may refuse night entry, pushing cutovers into business hours and needing the customer's approval for downtime." P 3, I 4, score 12; owner, site coordinator; response, collect access letters during the surveys.

## Approvals

Three blank fields: sponsor, project manager and date. Compass leaves them empty on purpose; a signature has to come from the person.

- **Good**: the sponsor signs before major spending starts. Log the sign-off, with its date, in the Decisions tab so it can be found later.
- **Mistakes**: the PM signs alone; an email saying "looks good" taken as approval and never recorded.
- **Note**: on customer-facing work, the customer usually signs the statement of work instead; the internal charter still needs your own sponsor's signature.

## In practice

- Fill in every Overview field on your current project, then generate the charter and read it as the sponsor would.
- Rewrite any objective that starts with a verb like "deploy" or "install" as an outcome with a date.
- Add three likely customer requests to Out of scope.
- Check the top five risks in the generated table each have an owner and a real response.
- After the sponsor signs, add the sign-off to Decisions.

title: Template guide: RACI
body:
The RACI template is the one built-in document that Compass deliberately leaves mostly empty. Compass knows your milestones, but it does not know who does what, and guessing would produce a matrix (matrice RACI) that looks finished and has been agreed by nobody. So it gives you the grid and leaves the letters to you and the people named in it. You download it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab, as Word, Markdown or PDF; Word is the useful one here, because you will edit it. For the meaning of each letter and the common traps, read [[raci-matrix]] first.

## Deliverables

The rows are the project's milestones. A project with no milestones gets five placeholder rows, Deliverable 1 to Deliverable 5.

- **Good**: rows that are results someone can sign off: a design, a site acceptance, a cutover plan, a handover pack, a go-live decision. Eight to fifteen rows is usually enough to cover the moments where accountability matters.
- **What to change**: milestones are events, and some of them are not deliverables ("pilot live" is an outcome of several deliverables). Rename such rows to the thing being produced or decided, split a row when two different people would sign its parts, and add rows for important decisions that are not milestones, such as a design change or a vendor substitution.
- **Mistakes**: rows that are activities ("weekly meeting", "testing"); fifty rows nobody will read.
- **Example**: "Wave 2 live" becomes two rows: "Wave 2 cutover plan" and "Wave 2 go / no-go".

## Roles

The columns are Sponsor, Project manager, Team, Vendor and Operations.

- **Good**: columns that match how your project is really organised. Split "Team" into the groups that actually do the work, such as solution architecture, provisioning and field services. On B2B work, add a column for the customer, because many deliverables need their input or signature.
- **Names or roles**: use roles in the columns and keep a short legend of who holds each role today. People change during a long rollout; roles rarely do.
- **Mistakes**: a column for every individual, which makes the table too wide to print; leaving out operations, who then refuse a handover they never agreed to.
- **Example**: Sponsor; Project manager; Solution architect; Provisioning; Install vendor; Customer IT; Operations.

## Filling the cells

Every cell starts blank. Fill them in a working session with the people named, not alone at your desk.

- **Good**: go row by row and ask the four questions: who does the work, whose name is on the result, who must be heard before it is final, and who needs to know afterwards. Then read down each column: a person with R's on half the rows is overloaded, and a column of only I's may not belong in the matrix.
- **Mistakes**: a C in every cell "to be inclusive", which slows every deliverable; the project manager as A on every row.
- **Example row**: "Handover to operations": Sponsor I, Project manager R, Solution architect C, Customer IT I, Operations A.

## One A per row

Compass prints a note under the table: one A per row. It is the rule that makes the matrix worth having.

- **Good**: every row has exactly one A, and that person has the authority to sign. If two people insist on the A, split the row by aspect (technical and commercial approval) or agree who breaks a tie.
- **Mistakes**: a row with no A, which tends to be the row that slips; two A's, which means a decision that bounces between two desks.
- **Check**: before sharing, scan the A's alone. Each one should be a name that person would recognise and accept.

## After the session

Save the agreed matrix with the project's documents. When a change moves an A, for example a new vendor takes over installation, record it in the Decisions tab and update the matrix the same week.

## In practice

- Generate the RACI for your current project and rename any row that is an event into the deliverable behind it.
- Add a customer column if the project has a customer.
- Book thirty minutes with the leads to fill the cells together.
- Check every row has exactly one A before sending it out.
- Put a review of the matrix on the agenda of the next phase-end meeting.

title: Template guide: RAID log
body:
The RAID log template prints the project's RAID tab as four tables, one per type, so you can send it to a working group, attach it to a gate pack or walk through it at a steering committee. Compass builds it on your device and you download it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab as Word, Markdown or PDF. Open risks and issues are included and closed ones are left out; risks come highest score first. The document is only as good as the log behind it, so most of the advice below is about what to type on the RAID tab. For how to run the log itself, see [[raid-log]].

## Risks

One row per open risk, with the columns Risk, P, I, Score, Owner and Response. P and I are the 1 to 5 probability and impact you set on the tab, and the score is P × I.

- **Good**: the text reads as cause, event and effect, so a reader can tell what would actually happen. Probability and impact use scales you agreed with the sponsor, not a fresh guess each week. The owner is one person, and the response says what is being done and by when.
- **Mistakes**: one-word risks ("Vendor"); scores that never move; "monitor" as the only response; the same risk written twice by two people.
- **Example**: "Router supply relies on a single distributor, so a shortage could delay wave 3 shipments by four weeks or more and push the last cutovers past the contract date." P 3, I 4, score 12. Owner: vendor manager. Response: confirm stock for waves 3 and 4 by 15 January and ask for a second source quote.

The trigger you record on the RAID tab, the early sign that a risk is about to happen, stays on the tab; mention it in the response when the reader needs to watch for it.

## Assumptions

One row per assumption, text only.

- **Good**: written so it can be proven wrong, with who confirms it and by when inside the text. An assumption that turns out false becomes an issue or a risk, so check them on a schedule rather than waiting.
- **Mistakes**: wishes ("the customer will be cooperative"); assumptions that were confirmed months ago and still sit in the log.
- **Example**: "The customer provides rack space and power at every site before its survey; the customer's facilities lead confirms site by site, wave 1 by 30 November."

## Issues

One row per open issue, with its text, impact, owner and response.

- **Good**: what happened, what it affects now, and what decision or action is needed. Impact uses the same 1 to 5 scale as risks. If an issue needs someone above you, say so in the response and follow your escalation path (see [[issues-and-escalation]]).
- **Mistakes**: issues kept open after they are fixed; future events logged as issues; an owner who has not been told.
- **Example**: "Twelve routers for wave 2 held at customs since 4 December; four cutovers cannot go ahead next week." Impact 4. Owner: vendor manager. Response: broker has the missing commercial invoice; new delivery date to be confirmed Friday; the four sites move to the next window if it slips.

## Dependencies

One row per dependency, with its text and owner.

- **Good**: names the other party, what they must deliver and the date you need it. The owner is the person on your side who chases it, not the other team.
- **Mistakes**: dependencies with no date; internal tasks of your own project listed as dependencies.
- **Example**: "The billing team's release must be in production before the first cutover, needed by 15 January, so that new service charges start correctly." Owner: project manager.

## Using the document

- Generate it on the morning of the meeting, so it matches the tab.
- For a steering committee, send only what needs its help; the full log suits the working group.
- Decisions taken while reviewing the log go into the Decisions tab; new actions become tasks with an owner and a due date.

## In practice

- Open the RAID tab and rewrite the three highest risks as cause, event and effect.
- Give every open item an owner, then generate the log and check no row has a blank owner.
- Confirm or close one assumption this week.
- Add a date to every dependency.
- Agree with the sponsor which score counts as high and use it in your next status report.

title: Template guide: status report
body:
The status report (rapport d'avancement) is the template you will generate most often. Compass shows it as a preview on the project's Report tab and builds it on your device for the period you pick: this week, the last two weeks, this month or custom dates. You download it as Word, Markdown or PDF; the same report also appears in the Templates list below the preview. Almost every section is filled from the project's own data, so a weak report usually points to something on the project page that needs attention, not to the document. What a good report says, and how to set RAG thresholds, is covered in [[status-reporting]]; this guide goes through the sections in order.

## Overall status

Three fields: the RAG, its reason, and the period.

- **Comes from**: the RAG and the RAG reason on the project page, and the range you chose.
- **Good**: a reason a busy executive can act on, with the trend: "Amber, getting worse: wave 2 equipment held at customs; four cutovers at risk next week."
- **Mistakes**: a blank reason, which leaves the reader guessing; a reason that describes activity ("working with vendor").

## Executive summary

On a project that allows cloud AI, "Write the summary with the copilot" drafts this section from the report's data. Otherwise, Compass prints the progress line: tasks done this period, done out of total with a percentage, and the number overdue.

- **Good**: three to five sentences: where the project stands, what changed since last time, what you need and from whom. Edit the copilot's draft or the progress line in Word until it says that.
- **Mistakes**: sending the bare task count to a sponsor; a summary that ends without the ask.

## Progress

A list of the tasks marked done within the period.

- **Good**: task titles that read as results ("Site acceptance signed, 6 of 12 wave 2 sites"), because the list is printed as written. Titles that work on your board also work here when they name an output.
- **Mistakes**: titles only you understand ("follow up w/ JP"); a period so long that the list runs to a page.

## Next steps

The open tasks due in the next two weeks.

- **Good**: the few things the reader would want to know are coming, with dates. If a key step is missing, it is usually missing a due date on the board.
- **Mistakes**: twenty routine tasks drowning the two that matter. Split or merge tasks on the board rather than editing the list every week.

## Milestones

A table of the project's milestones, each with its due date and a state: Done, Late, Due this period or Upcoming.

- **Good**: a short list of summary milestones with gates marked ◆ on the project page and their outcomes recorded in Decisions. A Late milestone should already have a line in the RAG reason and an item in the RAID log.
- **Mistakes**: a milestone shown Late for weeks with nothing said about it; done milestones never ticked, so they show as Late.

## Risks and issues

Two tables from the RAID tab: open risks, highest score first, and open issues.

- **Good**: every row has an owner and a real response. For a steering committee, trim the Word version to the risks that need its attention; the working group can have the full lists.
- **Mistakes**: risks nobody has rescored for a month; issues already resolved but never closed on the tab.

## Decisions needed

The project's pending change requests, by title.

- **Good**: each title says what decision is needed, so it can be read alone: "Approve two extra night cutover windows for wave 3". Put the most important one in the executive summary too.
- **Mistakes**: change requests left pending after a verbal decision; other decisions you need (a design choice, a budget release) left out. Add those as a line in Word, or log them as change requests if they change scope, time or cost.

## Decisions made

A table of the decisions logged in the Decisions tab during the period, with their dates.

- **Good**: decisions written so they stand alone: who decided what, and any condition attached. Gate outcomes belong here.
- **Mistakes**: decisions taken in meetings but never logged, so the report suggests nothing was decided.

## In practice

- Fill in the RAG reason on every active project before generating its report.
- Pick "Last 2 weeks" for a fortnightly report so the Progress list matches what the reader last saw.
- Rename three board tasks so they read as results.
- Close any RAID item that is no longer open, then regenerate.
- Log this week's decisions in the Decisions tab before sending the report.

title: Template guide: WBS outline
body:
The WBS outline template prints a numbered outline of the project from what Compass already holds: milestones as the top-level branches and tasks underneath them. You download it from the Templates list on the project's Report tab, as Word, Markdown or PDF. Be clear about what it is. A textbook work breakdown structure (structure de découpage du projet, SDP) is organised by deliverables; this outline is organised by time, because it groups tasks by the milestone they are due by. That makes it a strong check on your plan and a good first draft, but you will reshape it before calling it the project's WBS. The method behind a real WBS is in [[wbs-and-scheduling]].

## Milestone branches

Each milestone becomes a numbered branch: 1, 2, 3 and so on.

- **Good**: milestones that each close off a recognisable piece of the work, such as design approved, pilot live, each rollout wave live, handover done. When milestones match deliverables, the outline is already close to a real WBS.
- **Mistakes**: milestones that are only dates ("end of November") or meetings ("steering committee"), which give branches with no shape; one milestone at the end of the project, which puts every task in a single branch.
- **Example**: 1 Design approved; 2 Pilot of five sites live; 3 Wave 2 live; 4 Wave 3 live; 5 Handover to operations.

## Tasks under each milestone

Under each branch, Compass lists the tasks due on or before that milestone's date, numbered 1.1, 1.2 and onwards.

- **Good**: each task is a piece of work one person can own, with a clear output and a due date. Read every branch with the completeness test: if all these tasks are done, is the milestone really met? If the honest answer is "nearly", a task is missing. Testing, training, documentation, customer sign-off and decommissioning old services are the usual gaps.
- **Mistakes**: tasks so small that a branch runs to forty lines, which means the board is being used as a to-do list for the WBS; tasks so large ("do wave 2") that nobody can estimate them.
- **Example**: under 3 Wave 2 live: 3.1 confirm site readiness for 12 sites; 3.2 ship routers; 3.3 schedule cutover windows with the customer; 3.4 cut over sites; 3.5 obtain site acceptance; 3.6 stop billing on the old circuits.

When a task has slipped past its milestone's date, it lands under a later branch. Treat that as a signal: either the task is late, or the milestone is already at risk and belongs in the RAID log.

## Other work

Tasks that Compass could not place under any milestone are listed at the end under "Other work", for example tasks with no due date or due after the last milestone.

- **Good**: a short list of ongoing management work, such as weekly reporting or vendor meetings, which really does run across the whole project.
- **Mistakes**: a long Other work section. It usually means tasks are missing due dates, or a final milestone such as closure is missing from the plan.
- **What to do**: give the stray tasks dates, add the missing milestone, then generate the outline again.

## Turning the outline into a WBS

When you need a deliverable-based WBS, for a contract, a gate pack or a vendor's statement of work, take the Word version and reshape it:

- Regroup the branches by deliverable (design, equipment, site readiness, installs, integration, acceptance, project management) and move tasks into them.
- Check the 100% rule: everything in scope appears once, and nothing on the charter's out-of-scope list appears at all.
- Stop breaking down at work packages (lots de travail) one person can own and estimate.
- Add the estimates; three-point ranges work well here (see [[estimation-techniques]]).

On a project that allows cloud AI, the copilot's "Plan from scope" preset can propose a breakdown to work-package level with three-point estimates, working from the project's scope. Its proposals reach the board only when you choose "Add to the board", and the next outline will include them.

## In practice

- Generate the outline for your current project and count the tasks under Other work.
- Give every undated task a due date, or delete it if it no longer matters.
- Run the completeness test on the next milestone's branch and add what is missing.
- Check the last milestone is closure, not the final cutover.
- Turn the outline into a deliverable-based WBS before your next gate.

title: Glossary: English ↔ French PM terms
body:
Bell Business Markets projects run in two languages. A steering committee in Montréal may hold its meeting in French while the vendor's status report arrives in English, and a status report written for a Québec executive reads better in French. This glossary gives the French term a project manager is most likely to hear or need for each common English term, with a one-line meaning in Compass's own words. It is a working vocabulary, not a translation standard: where your organisation, a contract or the customer uses another term, follow them.

## How to read the table

- Terms are in alphabetical order by English. Search the library for either language to land here.
- Where Québec and France commonly use different words, both are given and marked: **(QC)** for usage common in Québec and in Canadian French generally, **(FR)** for usage common in France. A term with no mark is used on both sides.
- Where two French terms are listed without marks, both are in common use.
- Acronyms in brackets are the English ones (CPI, SPI, WBS). French acronyms are given only where they are in everyday use, such as ENS for an SLA or COPIL in France.
- PRINCE2 and PMBOK have official French editions whose wording sometimes differs from everyday usage; in a certification context, use the edition's own terms.

## The terms

| English | Français | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Accept (risk response) | accepter | Choosing to live with a risk, with or without money or time set aside for it. |
| Acceptance | acceptation | The customer or sponsor formally agreeing that a deliverable is what was asked for. |
| Acceptance criteria | critères d'acceptation | The checks a deliverable has to pass before anyone signs for it. |
| Action item | action à réaliser | A piece of follow-up work from a meeting, with one owner and a date. |
| Action log | registre des actions | The running list of open and closed action items for a project. |
| Activity | activité | A scheduled piece of work with a duration, smaller than a work package. |
| Actual cost (AC) | coût réel | What has really been spent on the work done so far. |
| Agenda | ordre du jour | The list of topics, in order, that a meeting will cover. |
| Agile | agile | Delivering in short cycles and adjusting the plan from what each cycle teaches. |
| Agreement | entente (QC); accord (FR) | A settled arrangement between parties, written or not. |
| Analogous estimating | estimation par analogie | Estimating from the actual figures of a similar past project. |
| Assumption | hypothèse | A belief the plan depends on that has not been checked yet. |
| Assumption log | registre des hypothèses | Where assumptions are listed with who confirms each one and by when. |
| Audit | audit; vérification (QC, public sector) | An independent check that work or records meet a standard. |
| Avoid (risk response) | éviter | Changing the plan so a threat can no longer occur. |
| Backlog | carnet de produit (QC); backlog (FR) | The ordered list of work still to be done on a product. |
| Baseline | référence de base | The agreed snapshot of scope, schedule or cost that you measure progress against. |
| Benefit | bénéfice; avantage | A measurable gain the organisation expects from the project's outcome. |
| Benefits realization | réalisation des bénéfices | Making sure promised benefits actually arrive, often after the project ends. |
| Bottom-up estimating | estimation ascendante | Estimating each work package and adding them up. |
| Budget | budget | The money approved for the project, usually split by phase or category. |
| Budget at completion (BAC) | budget à l'achèvement | The total planned budget for all the work in scope. |
| Buffer | tampon; marge de sécurité | Time or money held back to absorb variation without moving a commitment. |
| Business analyst | analyste d'affaires (QC); analyste métier (FR) | The person who turns business needs into clear requirements. |
| Business case | dossier d'affaires (QC); étude de rentabilité (FR) | The argument that a project is worth its cost and risk. |
| Business requirement | exigence d'affaires (QC); exigence métier (FR) | A need stated from the business's point of view rather than the system's. |
| Change control | maîtrise des changements; contrôle des changements | The process that assesses and decides proposed changes to an agreed baseline. |
| Change control board | comité des changements | The group with authority to approve or reject change requests. |
| Change freeze | gel des changements | A period when no changes are allowed, often around a cutover or year end. |
| Change management (organisational) | gestion du changement | Helping people adopt a new way of working; not the same as change control. |
| Change request | demande de changement (QC); demande de modification (FR) | A written ask to change what was agreed on scope, time, cost or quality. |
| Closing | clôture | The final phase: acceptance, handover, contract and financial closure. |
| Closure report | rapport de clôture | The document that records how the project ended against its goals. |
| Communication plan | plan de communication | Who receives which information, how often, through which channel and from whom. |
| Configuration management | gestion de la configuration | Keeping track of versions of deliverables and documents and what changed. |
| Constraint | contrainte | A fixed limit the project must work within, such as a date or budget. |
| Contingency reserve | réserve pour aléas; réserve pour imprévus | Money or time in the baseline kept for risks you already know about. |
| Continuous improvement | amélioration continue | Small, regular changes to how work is done, based on what is learned. |
| Contract | contrat | A legally binding agreement on what will be delivered and paid. |
| Cost baseline | référence de base des coûts | The approved, time-phased budget used to measure cost performance. |
| Cost performance index (CPI) | indice de performance des coûts | Earned value divided by actual cost; below 1 means overspending. |
| Cost variance (CV) | écart de coût | Earned value minus actual cost; negative means over budget. |
| Cost-plus contract | contrat à prix coûtant majoré | The buyer pays the seller's costs plus an agreed fee or margin. |
| Critical path | chemin critique | The chain of dependent work that sets the earliest finish date. |
| Customer | client | The organisation that pays for and receives the result. |
| Cutover | basculement; bascule | The moment service moves from the old setup to the new one. |
| Daily scrum | mêlée quotidienne (QC); daily, point quotidien (FR) | A short daily team check on progress toward the sprint goal. |
| Dashboard | tableau de bord | A one-screen view of a few key measures. |
| Deadline | échéance; date limite | The date by which something must be finished. |
| Decision log | registre des décisions | The dated record of decisions, who made them and any conditions. |
| Decomposition | décomposition | Breaking work into smaller parts until each can be owned and estimated. |
| Definition of done | définition de « terminé » | The shared checklist an item must meet before it counts as finished. |
| Deliverable | livrable | Something tangible the project has to hand over, such as a design, a working site or a report. |
| Dependency | dépendance | A link where one piece of work needs another to start or finish first. |
| Deployment | déploiement | Rolling a solution out to its users or sites. |
| Downtime | interruption de service; temps d'arrêt | The period during which a service is unavailable. |
| Duration | durée | Working time an activity takes from start to finish. |
| Earned value (EV) | valeur acquise | The budgeted value of the work actually completed. |

## In practice

- Before your next French-language steering committee, check the terms on your slides against this table: échéancier, portée, livrable, jalon.
- Write the meeting's decisions in the language the meeting was held in, and keep the same term for the same thing throughout a document.
- In emails to Québec colleagues, prefer the (QC) terms: courriel, rencontre, soumission, gabarit.
- When a vendor's French term differs from yours, agree one term per project and put it in the communication plan.
- Ask the copilot to write a French version of a status summary, then check its terms here before sending.
